detail.abstract: Leadership development literature has historically been organized around adult, organizational, and post-appointment contexts, leaving a conceptual gap in how leadership capacity forms during adolescence and early adulthood. This paper proposes the ARCHIVE framework, a developmental model that organizes leadership formation in Generation Z around seven interdependent competencies: Adaptability, Resilience, Communication, Humility, Integrity, Vision, and Emotional Quotient. Drawing on a practitioner account of leadership development articulated in The Leadership Feed (Nagaraj, 2024) and situating that account within established scholarship on transformational, authentic, and adaptive leadership, the paper argues that these seven competencies are best cultivated not through formal instruction but through the ordinary developmental settings already available to young people in school projects, sport, cultural events, peer networks, and the management of their own time and commitments. For each competency, the paper specifies its conceptual content, its observable behaviours, and the everyday contexts in which it can be deliberately practised. The framework is offered as a scaffold for educators, programme designers, and early-career mentors who seek a common vocabulary for leadership formation, and as a set of testable propositions for future empirical work. The paper closes by acknowledging its conceptual rather than empirical status and outlining a research agenda for validating the framework.

detail.title:
Employment and Labour Markets
Examining Temporary Employment in EU Member States: A  Longitudinal Perspective
detail.abstract: The report examines temporary employment in EU member states between 2004 and 2023 using longitudinal EU-SILC data. It traces trends in temporary employment across countries, highlighting persistent differences: Spain and Portugal maintain high levels, while Austria and the Netherlands exhibit lower and more stable shares. The paper also examines variation by sex, age, and education, showing that temporary employment is concentrated among young workers, women, and lower-educated individuals, who also face weaker prospects of exiting temporary work. Beyond describing trends, it analyses transitions between temporary and permanent jobs, as well as movements into other labour market states. It combines descriptive evidence with econometric analysis, including fixed-effects models that account for unobserved individual differences. The results suggest that temporary employment is, on average, positively associated with obtaining a permanent job in the following period, supporting the steppingstone argument. However, this relationship varies considerably across countries and groups and is weaker in more segmented labour markets. Finally, the report also examines how labour market institutions, such as employment protection legislation and active labour market policies, relate to transitions out of temporary work. The findings suggest that these institutional factors do not have a uniform or robust effect and are difficult to separate from broader labour market conditions.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Private Tutoring, and Class Reproduction A Political-Economy Hypothesis and Evidence Map Using Korea as a Case

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Private Tutoring, and Class Reproduction A Political-Economy Hypothesis and Evidence Map Using Korea as a Case
detail.abstract: South Korea (hereafter Korea) exhibits internationally very high private-tutoring (shadow-education) participation and spending while simultaneously recording one of the world's lowest fertility rates, so that its school-age population is contracting rapidly. In 2025 total private-tutoring spending, the participation rate, and weekly hours all declined, yet per-participating-student spending actually rose and the income-based spending gap persisted. The fall in the aggregate therefore cannot by itself be read as a structural easing of tutoring dependence or of class inequality. It is at this moment that generative artificial intelligence (AI) enters as an educational resource. The dominant policy narrative expects AI to lower tutoring dependence and dissolve gaps; this study argues against that expectation. Its claim is the following hypothesis: AI is a complement to existing educational capital, and its learning effect will be larger the larger the capital a household already holds (a positive interaction). High-capital households combine high-cost tutoring, higher-performing AI, and parental cultural capital and convert these into a larger learning effect, whereas low-capital households, even with access to the same cheapened AI, lack the complementary inputs to convert it, so that under a no-intervention condition the gap may widen. The study joins the political economy of AI-gain capture (Acemoglu–Restrepo, Korinek–Stiglitz) to the theory of educational reproduction (Bourdieu, Chetty) at the household and private-tutoring layer, and uses Korea — a country of internationally high tutoring participation/spending and a large income gap — as an extreme diagnostic case. Because panel statistics on AI use, spending, and learning outcomes by income decile are currently absent (though class differences in adolescents' generative-AI use experience are already observed — see §4), the joint claim is presented not as an established fact but as a falsifiable hypothesis, supported by theory and adjacent data, with explicit statement of what data would confirm or refute it. The claim is not deterministic — it states a pressure toward widening under the absence of policy intervention, not a physical necessity. In the policy analysis the study shows that AI policy can narrow the conversion gap but that its effect is bounded by three constraints — prior knowledge, teacher capacity, and household capital — and that the residual passes to the problem of distribution. Finally, the study directly concedes the strongest causal evidence that AI can compress gaps in short-term task performance (Noy–Zhang 2023; Brynjolfsson et al. 2025), while defending its hypothesis on the time horizon of long-run learning formation and conversion, and distinguishing itself from adjacent prior work at the level of analysis (household, private tutoring, intergenerational reproduction).

title: The Superstar Buyer Penalty during Financial Crises: Evidence from Firm-to-Firm Trade Data

detail.title: The Superstar Buyer Penalty during Financial Crises: Evidence from Firm-to-Firm Trade Data
detail.abstract: This paper documents that firms connected with superstar buyers experience larger real losses when hit by financial shocks. Using Italian loan-level data, we show that firms most affected by the credit crunch induced by the 2011 sovereign debt crisis reduced exports more sharply. Importantly, export declines were larger for exporters connected with foreign superstar buyers prior to the shock. This amplification is explained by superstar buyers disproportionately reallocating purchases away from exposed suppliers, which also experienced lower sales and employment. Partial-equilibrium aggregation implies that this superstar penalty explains around one-third of the aggregate negative effect of the credit supply shock.

detail.title: State Tax Enforcement of Section 1031 Proximate Exchanges

publicationDetails.detailsText: Brooklyn Law School, Legal Studies Paper No. 814
publicationDetails.journalName: Brooklyn Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: 26 UC Davis Bus. L. J. 136 (2026) (with Lovepreet Kaur)

detail.abstract:
A section 1031 proximate exchange occurs when partners desire to transfer partnership property, separate, and separately complete section 1031 exchanges with their respective individual shares of sale proceeds. A section 1031 proximate exchange also occurs when an exchanger desires to acquire property as part of an intended section 1031 exchange and contribute it to a partnership. These transactions are often referred to as “drop-and-swaps” or “swap-and-drops.” The United States Tax Court has established the proximate-exchange principle: “[A] trade of property A for property B, both of like kind, may be preceded by the tax-free acquisition of Property A at the front end, or succeeded by a tax-free transfer of property B on the back end.” Despite this well-established principle, some commentators and advisors still hesitate to rely upon it when advising property owners with respect to proximate exchanges. More troubling, is the disregard of the principle by states that adopt federal income tax rules as their state law. Such disregard by states has many negative tax consequences.

California has most blatantly disregarded the proximate-exchange principle with predictable results. The California Franchise Tax Board (California FTB), the state’s tax enforcement agency, flouts the proximate-exchange principle, and the California Office of Tax Appeals (California OTA), an independent body created by the California legislature to hear taxpayer appeals from positions taken by the California FTB. The California OTA applied the proximate-exchange principle in some cases but more recently failed to apply it in other cases. The result of the different results published by the California OTA is guidance that lacks internal consistency and is inconsistent with the federal proximate-exchange principle. This lack of uniformity creates many undesirable results, including taxpayer confusion, high-cost alternative structures, inequitable tax-planning opportunities that favor high-value transactions, structured transactions that introduce serious non-tax risks into ownership that would not otherwise be present, and sends a horrible message to taxpayers regarding state tax enforcement.

This Article reviews the federal law regarding section 1031 proximate exchanges, showing that federal law overwhelmingly supports granting section 1031 nonrecognition to proximate exchanges. Federal courts present both sound technical and policy reasons for granting section 1031 nonrecognition to such transactions. By contrast, California deviates from federal law in this area with blatant technical and policy deficiencies. This Article reviews the California rulings, showing their inconsistent treatment of section 1031 proximate exchanges and further revealing their technical deficiencies. That analysis shows that California (1) does not apply federal tax law to its detriment; (2) presents a substance-over-form analysis that collapses on itself by elevating formal aspects of proximate-exchange structures over substance when convenient to its desired outcome and otherwise applying the principle haphazardly; (3) commits blatant technical errors in its opinions; and (4) and disregards the purposes of nonrecognition provisions that federal courts rely upon. After showing the shortcomings of California rulings, the Article considers other state decisions and presents suggestions for fixing the problems caused by the California rulings.

detail.title: The impact of spousal Social Security claiming decisions on the financial shock of widowhood

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract: This paper presents evidence suggesting that delayed Social Security claiming by husbands-resulting in an actuarially enhanced benefitattenuates the financial shock of widowhood for their wives. Under Social Security survivor benefit rules, primary earners (usually husbands) pass on the actuarial adjustments from delayed claiming to their surviving spouses. Using a staggered difference-indifferences approach, I find women whose husbands delayed claiming to full retirement age or later face a post-widowhood increase of 6.9 percentage points in the probability of falling below the 5th percentile of the pre-widowhood income distribution. This effect is almost 12 percent smaller for each year of delayed claiming by the husband (though the attenuation is concentrated in the first 4 years of widowhood). The general findings are robust to instrumenting for the husband's claiming age using the loosening of the retirement earnings test in 2000-a policy change that incentivized earlier claiming.

detail.title: 401(k) Participant Behavior: Knowledge and Action

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
Today’s 401(k) environment is characterized by significant buzz about lifetime income. The 401(k) system has reached the stage where individuals are approaching and entering retirement having spent a significant portion (maybe even all) of their work lives participating in a 401(k) plan. This naturally drives an increasing focus on helping participants convert retirement savings to retirement income, something that wasn’t a focus when the first plans were established in the early 1980s.

Previous research by Nuveen and the TIAA Institute examined 401(k) participant perspectives on generating retirement income from 401(k) savings, including the value of in-plan annuities. This report complements that analysis by using data from the 2025 Nuveen and TIAA Institute Participant Sentiment Survey on Lifetime Income to examine 401(k) participant behavior in the current environment.

This report also examines retirement fluency and longevity literacy among 401(k) participants. An individual’s standard of living over the course of retirement depends on more than accumulated savings at the time of retirement and how that savings is subsequently used. So helping 401(k) participants achieve retirement income security involves more than providing plan-related guidance. Individuals make a range of decisions, while working and after retiring, that matter, and they make those decisions not knowing how long their retirement will last. Retirement fluency and longevity literacy enable appropriate decision-making in this context.

title: The Disappearing Overnight Drift
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Copenhagen Business School and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: The Disappearing Overnight Drift

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In a 2021 Liberty Street Economics post, we documented the “overnight drift”—a large, persistent return to holding U.S. equity futures in the narrow window between 2:00 and 3:00 a.m. Eastern time, when European equity markets open. Five additional years of data later, that pattern appears to have faded: the 2:00–3:00 window that previously generated roughly 3.7 percent per annum has averaged close to zero since 2021. In this post, we revisit the overnight drift in light of the post-publication sample and use our inventory-risk framework to ask which of three observable channels—the dispersion of closing order imbalances, the level of return variance, or the risk-bearing capacity of liquidity providers—accounts for the change.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/07/the-disappearing-overnight-drift/

detail.title: Central bank communication: New data and stylized facts from a century of Fed speeches

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Working Paper No. 06/2026

detail.abstract: Drawing on a novel dataset of more than 10,000 speeches from 1914 to 2024, we track the evolution of Federal Reserve communication and identify three stylized facts. (1) Although the overall volume of speeches has declined over the past decade, the composition of Fed communication has remained notably consistent for forty years, with Federal Reserve Bank (FRB) presidents accounting for the majority of public engagements. Variation in communicative participation is driven primarily by dispositional factors, including professional background, gender, and other speaker-specific idiosyncrasies, rather than the particular time frame in which the speeches were delivered. (2) While governors' communication reacts to financial stability, FRB presidents' schedules remain decoupled from both regional shifts in their districts and broader macroindicators. (3) A "complexity paradox" has emerged: while the syntactic structure simplifies during crises, the conceptual density increases. When adjusted for abstractness, the communication patterns of governors and FRB presidents appear remarkably similar.

detail.abstract: Scotland has a fascinating and, in many ways, unexplored history of trust law. Scotland is a mixed legal system that combines elements both of civil law and common law. And yet trusts thrive in Scotland and have done so for many centuries. This paper provides an overview of the development of trust law in Scotland. It aims to show that Scottish trust law represents a fascinating case study for any comparative legal scholar. While there has been inevitable cross-fertilization between England and Wales and Scotland, which might explain some of the significant structural and practical similarities in their law of trusts, trusts in Scotland have their own distinct history and their own distinctive features. This paper will further illustrate that Scotland has recently overhauled its trust law partly drawing on foreign source material or transplanting new foreign concepts into its own jurisdiction. At the same time, Scotland and, in particular, the way in which it conceptualises trusts through the dual patrimony theory has also influenced debates elsewhere.

title: Decomposing the 2020s Asian Surplus: Demographic Residuals, Cyclical Policy, and Sectoral Concentration

detail.title: Decomposing the 2020s Asian Surplus: Demographic Residuals, Cyclical Policy, and Sectoral Concentration
detail.abstract: The global current-account imbalance has compressed into a single Asian surplus dominated by China, with a customs goods surplus of approximately $1.2 trillion in 2024 and a manufacturing surplus near 2 percent of world GDP. Recent commentary attributes this configuration to managed exchange rates, capital controls, and state-directed credit, in tension with a literature that locates persistent imbalances in demographic structure. We test where the recent Asian surplus loads after pinning down the demographic prediction. Using the 140-country panel of Peters (2024a)-N = 5,455 country-years across 185 country units, 1990-2024, with the income-conditional Paper 1 baseline (Z₁ × log GDP per capita = 0.86, p = 0.018) producing the demographic residuals analyzed throughout-UN Comtrade HS-2 chapter data for Chinese exports, and IMF SDMX 3.0 customs and balance-of-payments goods balances, we estimate four propositions. First, the residual current-account surplus in aging Asia after the demographic baseline loads on within-country real exchange rate deviation (β =-9.4, p < 0.001) and reserve accumulation (β = +0.19, p = 0.007), with R² rising from 0.015 globally to 0.139 in the Asia surplus subsample; China and Japan run residuals of 5.4 and 6.1 percentage points above demographic prediction. Second, the change in export-price level is a strong predictor of the current account that is missing from standard specifications: adding it raises R² from 0.146 to 0.237 and strengthens the income-conditional demographic interaction (Z₁ × log GDP per capita: 0.86, p = 0.018 → 1.07, p < 0.001), with Harberger-Laursen-Metzler endogeneity preventing a clean causal claim. Third, China-origin exports of vehicles and machinery exhibit positive demographic gravity (β = +0.37 and +0.30, both p < 0.01) into aging-rich destinations, with Germany and Belgium among the top 2024 destination overshoots; chemicals and aircraft show no demographic gravity. Fourth, China's customs-minus-balance-of-payments goods balance gap surged from approximately zero (-0.09 percentage points) in 2018 to a peak of +1.42 percentage points in 2023, settling at +0.98 percentage points ($184 billion) in 2024, while the crosscountry mechanism, that capital controls amplify the gap, runs the wrong direction (Z₁ × KAOPEN = +0.32, p = 0.020); the crosscountry pattern is dominated by multinational-residence reclassification (Ireland, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Singapore, Switzerland), not by capital controls. The simple peg-versus-float distinction does not moderate the demographic-real exchange rate relationship (Z₁ × is_peg =-0.002, p = 0.82). The Asian surplus that motivates current commentary sits as a residual on top of a demographic baseline that is not refuted by these tests; the residual is sectorally concentrated in autos and capital goods and reflects cyclical policy responsiveness, not the structural undervaluation magnitudes the commentary proposes.

title: Demographic Persistence and Compositional Drift in EU External Imbalances through 2050: A Note Responding to Darvas et al (2026)

detail.title: Demographic Persistence and Compositional Drift in EU External Imbalances through 2050: A Note Responding to Darvas et al (2026)
detail.abstract:
Darvas et al (2026, Bruegel WP 07/2026) document that the EU27 current-account surplus has averaged 2-3 percent of GDP since 2010, identify four chronic-surplus countries (Germany, Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden), and project the surplus to persist at 2.5-3.0 percent of GDP through approximately 2035. They attribute the residual EBA gaps for the four chronic-surplus countries (DK +15 pp, NL +8 pp, SE +5 pp, DE +4 pp above the EBA-implied norm) to "unobservable structural characteristics.

" This note quantifies three demographic-channel results that engage their persistence claim, their compositional analysis, and their EBA-residual finding directly. First, applying the global income-interacted current-account specification of Peters (2026a) to UN WPP demographic projections yields a GDP-weighted EU27 demographic contribution to CA that changes by only-0.13 pp/GDP between 2024 and 2050; the implied persistence forecast is +2.26 pp/GDP at 2050, within Darvas et al's 2.5-3.0 pp range. Second, the aggregate flatness conceals substantial within-EU compositional drift: demographics push the surplus four flat-to-rising (DNK +0.47, SWE +0.63 over the horizon) while pushing the southern deficit countries deeper into deficit (ITA-0.90, ESP-1.19). Third, on a 31-country EU+UK+NO+CH+IS sectoral B.9 panel, the demographic-funded-pension interaction is +10.0 (p < 0.01) on the corporate-sector net lending channel, identifying corporate retention as the mechanism through which funded-pension systems route demographic savings outward. The income interaction (Z₁ × log GDP/cap) directly accounts for approximately 1 pp/country of the chronic-surplus residual; the remainder reflects specification differences from EBA we do not isolate. The note's central empirical claim is that demographics deliver near-zero mean reversion at the EU27 aggregate while widening the within-EU imbalance, supporting Darvas et al's investment-raising rather than savings-reducing policy emphasis.

title:
When Bread Rebinds: 
A Leontief Theory of Symbolic Mandate Exhaustion

detail.title:
When Bread Rebinds: 
A Leontief Theory of Symbolic Mandate Exhaustion
detail.abstract: I develop a theory of symbolic mandate exhaustion. Voters require both material security ("bread," c) and social meaning ("meaning," m), and the two are poor substitutes near important social baselines, so welfare is governed by the lower of the two. When meaning is the initially binding constraint, a political movement can raise welfare by supplying recognition, dignity, identity validation, and narrative repair. Credible entry, however, requires a minimum viable symbolic package rather than a finely tuned marginal adjustment: a challenger must differentiate itself enough to be read as a distinct political type. Conditional on entry the movement supplies this package and devotes its remaining capacity to material delivery. When the resulting allocation leaves bread below repaired meaning, entry raises welfare and switches the binding constraint from meaning to bread. Past that switch, further symbolic supply has zero marginal welfare value in the Leontief limit and sharply diminished value under low-substitution preferences. The movement's symbolic mandate is exhausted unless it can convert recognition into reconstruction. A reference-dependent extension shows when exhaustion of the instrument becomes outright decay of support. Brief illustrations distinguish recognition movements that exhaust once they govern from those whose mandate persists because the material delivery test has not arrived.

title: Mapping the Formal Capacity for Urban Pest Control in Brazil: Private Provision, Public Procurement, and the Geography of Coverage

detail.title: Mapping the Formal Capacity for Urban Pest Control in Brazil: Private Provision, Public Procurement, and the Geography of Coverage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used secondary, aggregated administrative data and did not involve direct contact with human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We build the first municipality-level account of formal pest-control capacity in Brazil. Linking the universe of 81,841 pest-control establishments to the 11,048 contracts on the federal procurement portal over 2015-2026, we find capacity that is near-universal in population but thin in territory. Establishments operate in 68% of municipalities yet reach 94% of the population, while just 26% of municipalities have ever signed a municipal pest-control contract. Both margins rise steeply with city size, and the private market reaches more than twice as many municipalities as the public sector contracts in, so the binding policy margin is procurement rather than supply. Recorded contracting concentrates after the 2021 procurement law. Conditional correlations and an exploratory event study find capacity positively associated with arbovirus burden, because firms locate where transmission is high, which identifies reverse causality rather than a protective effect. We read formal pest control as measurable local adaptation infrastructure.

title: No Evidence of Source-country De-Risking in Bilateral EM Equity: Income-conditional Allocation Patterns from 40 OECD Economies

detail.title: No Evidence of Source-country De-Risking in Bilateral EM Equity: Income-conditional Allocation Patterns from 40 OECD Economies
detail.abstract: Does population aging in wealthy economies systematically reduce their equity exposure to high-volatility emerging market (EM) destinations? Standard portfolio lifecycle theory predicts yes. This paper tests that prediction using bilateral portfolio equity holdings from 40 OECD source countries to 25 EM destinations over 2001-2023 (15,060 dyad-year observations), exploiting within-dyad variation via a gravity framework with dyad and year fixed effects. The de-risking hypothesis is rejected throughout: no specification produces the negative net demographic effect that the de-risking prediction requires at OECD income levels. The income-conditional mechanism of Peters (2024a)-that aging predicts capital outflows, not inflows, from high-income economies-generates a positive GLS point estimate for EM equity holdings at all observed OECD incomes (net Z₁ effect = +12 to +15), but this finding is not robust: cluster-robust standard errors with 34 source clusters yield a bootstrap 95% CI of [-100, +21] that includes zero, predetermined demographics (5-year lag) are null, and flow specifications show no significant demographic effect in either direction. The paper's primary contribution is therefore the rejection of de-risking rather than the confirmation of positive accumulation; the positive GLS point estimate is consistent with the income-conditional lifecycle mechanism but cannot be distinguished from zero with the available source-country variation. Heterogeneity tests find no differential reduction toward high-beta EM destinations, further contradicting the de-risking hypothesis.

title: "Is This Just a Street?" Estimating the Economic Impact of an Education-Led Urban Corridor in India
affiliations: Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: "Is This Just a Street?" Estimating the Economic Impact of an Education-Led Urban Corridor in India

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve medical research, clinical interventions, or the collection of sensitive personal data from human participants. The research was based on field observations, publicly observable commercial activity, publicly available information, and informal discussions with business stakeholders. No personally identifiable information was collected, and all findings are presented in aggregate form. Therefore, formal ethics committee approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
Urban economic research has traditionally focused on cities, industries, and large-scale infrastructure projects, often overlooking the economic significance of localized commercial corridors. This study examines KIIT Road, a 1.5-kilometer urban corridor in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, India, and investigates its role as an education-driven economic ecosystem. Anchored by the Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology (KIIT), the area has evolved into a dense commercial hub comprising retail establishments, food and beverage outlets, hospitality services, rental accommodations, and informal businesses that cater primarily to students, faculty members, and visitors.

Using a bottom-up revenue estimation framework based on field observations, business mapping, stakeholder interactions, and category-wise economic modeling, this study estimates the annual economic output generated by businesses operating along KIIT Road. The analysis suggests that the corridor generates between ₹240 crore and ₹462 crore in annual economic activity while supporting substantial direct and indirect employment across formal and informal sectors.

The study further compares KIIT Road with selected global urban economic corridors and highlights the unique characteristics of education-led commercial development in emerging urban centers. The findings demonstrate how higher education institutions can function as economic anchors, stimulating entrepreneurship, employment generation, real estate development, and localized business growth. By focusing on a single street-level ecosystem, this research contributes to the literature on urban economics, economic geography, and education-driven development, while offering insights for policymakers, urban planners, and researchers interested in understanding the economic impact of university-centered urban environments.

title: The Site of Paths: Local-to-Global Failure in Path-Generated Choice
affiliations: and University of Florence

detail.title: The Site of Paths: Local-to-Global Failure in Path-Generated Choice

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is theoretical and does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, interviews, surveys, experiments, or case-study subjects requiring ethics approval or informed consent.

detail.abstract: Standard choice theory takes the domain of alternatives, the ranking of outcomes, the continuity of the evaluating subject, and the space over which a plan is defined as primitive data, available before deliberation begins. This paper collects four results, each developed independently and by different formal means, that treat these objects instead as generated along admissible paths-and that ask, in four different settings, whether the coarse, endpoint-level description available after the fact recovers the finer structure that produced it. Comparability between states is generated by witnessed routes, and an Arrow-type impossibility follows from the aggregation not of rankings but of witnesses. Accessibility to a future is generated by the weighted mass of practicable and conceivable paths toward it, and an endpoint can remain formally describable while becoming effectively unreachable when the bridge-worlds sustaining the path are suppressed. First-personal evaluative continuity across a transformative choice is generated by an admissible counterpart relation between situated evaluators, and can fail not on any single transition but only around a cycle of transitions, a failure invisible to any pairwise analysis and identified here as a genuinely cyclic monodromy obstruction, naturally expressible in the language of holonomy but not equivalent to the vanishing of a Čech H 1-class. The space of complete alternatives generated by a finite-scope, singularly selective plan is topologically thinclosed and nowhere dense-even when it has the cardinality of the continuum, and the minimum number of such plans needed to exhaust the space of alternatives is a cardinal characteristic of the continuum, independent of the standard axioms of set theory. We show that these four failures of local-to-global reconstruction do not reduce to a single mathematical phenomenon dressed in four notations: they occupy genuinely different registers-cyclic monodromy, connectivity of a witness nerve, persistence along a closure filtration, and cardinal covering of a meagre ideal-on the same underlying site of admissible paths. We state this asymmetry as a result rather than concealing it, and identify the transport movement as the one in which the new formal apparatus is not descriptive but generative: it proves a theorem the arc-local theory cannot state.

title: A Taxonomy of Economic Literature Based on Paradigm Disruption and Methodological Utility
affiliations: International Islamic University Malaysia

detail.title: A Taxonomy of Economic Literature Based on Paradigm Disruption and Methodological Utility
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a five-tier taxonomy of economic literature based on paradigm disruption and methodological utility. By shifting focus from citation-based metrics to epistemic purpose and the nature of scholarly debate, the framework provides a functional classification of economic research. The five tiers are: (1) Paradigm-Shifting and Scholarly Debate, (2) Pure Economic Theory, (3) Methodological and Econometric Tooling, (4) Empirical Snapshots and Applied Policy Research, and (5) Knowledge Synthesis and Meta-Analytical Reviews. The paper defends this taxonomy as a more realistic representation of the division of labor in modern economic science and explores the implications of this framework for understanding the depreciation of empirical work and the evolution of economic thought. This taxonomy addresses the limitations of standard journal impact factors by focusing on the intensity of reader debates and the distinct roles researchers play within the discipline. The framework is grounded in the philosophy of science, drawing on Kuhnian paradigm theory and Lakatosian research programmes to justify the hierarchical structure of the classification.

title: Assessing Urban Quality of Life: Developing the Criteria for Saudi Cities

detail.title: Assessing Urban Quality of Life: Developing the Criteria for Saudi Cities

declarations.funderStatement: The Deputyship for Research & Innovation, Ministry of Education in Saudi Arabia funded research work through the project number SS-302 (through the initiative of social sciences number of the contract 4600000110).

detail.abstract: Urban quality of life (QOL) is a complex and multidimensional concept. A wide range of urban QOL assessment tools has been developed worldwide to measure and monitor the quality of urban life taking into account the particular conditions of cities/regions and the needs of their residents. This study aims to develop an urban QOL assessment tool appropriate for the context of Saudi Arabia (SA). For this purpose, this study developed and used a structured approach that consists of an in-depth analysis of 21 urban QOL assessment tools in use worldwide, combined with focus group analysis and feedback from a panel of experts. The results revealed that there is a lack of consensus among the existing tools regarding the usage of QOL indicators and domains, and that the majority of the tools demonstrate a lack of proper coverage of QOL subdomains. The results also show wide variations in the number of indicators used and that most of the examined tools are using objective measurable indicators. This study has identified 67 indicators distributed across 13 domains that constitute the core criteria of the proposed QOL assessment tool. The selected indicators and domains cover all the attributes of urban QOL and are evaluated by experts as important criteria to assess/measure QOL. Moreover, the results demonstrate the advantage of the developed framework and comprehensive list of criteria (CLC) as a structured and efficient approach to design better QOL assessment tools.

title: The Protective Myth as a Mechanism of Symbolic Influence: Sympathy, Silence, and the Social Cost of Criticism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Protective Myth as a Mechanism of Symbolic Influence: Sympathy, Silence, and the Social Cost of Criticism
detail.abstract:
This article develops the concept of the protective myth as a mechanism of symbolic influence. A protective myth is a narrative structure through which vulnerability, historical memory, cultural refinement, and moral injury become socially guarded. Such a myth does not necessarily begin as deception. It may contain genuine suffering, legitimate sensitivity, historical trauma, cultural beauty, and real experiences of misunderstanding. Its political function emerges when this vulnerability becomes difficult to question without incurring moral, emotional, reputational, or institutional cost. 
The central argument is that power does not always expand through command, coercion, wealth, propaganda, or direct persuasion. In some social and political environments, influence grows through sympathy, guilt, reverence, caution, and the fear of appearing insensitive. A protected actor may become difficult to criticize not because criticism is necessarily false, but because criticism begins to appear morally improper, culturally shallow, emotionally careless, socially crude, or politically dangerous. 
This study is conceptual and interpretive. It does not diagnose any people, culture, society, religion, nation, or historical community. Instead, it identifies a recurring political- psychological mechanism: the transformation of vulnerability into moral authority, moral authority into sympathy, sympathy into hesitation, hesitation into silence, and silence into influence. The article situates this mechanism within discussions of symbolic power, strategic narrative, moral capital, political psychology, identity protection, discourse, and the social cost of criticism.
The article argues that some actors expand influence not despite their protected story, but through it. Their fragility becomes a language. Their memory becomes a shield. Their refinement becomes a form of authority. Their pain becomes difficult to question. Over time, the boundary between empathy and submission, respect and silence, cultural sensitivity and political caution may become increasingly blurred.
By reframing influence as an arrangement of emotional relations rather than merely a strategy of communication, this article contributes to the study of symbolic power, political psychology, identity narratives, and informal mechanisms of social discipline.

title: Urban Transformation and Environmental Sustainability in Dhaka, Bangladesh: A Comparative Policy Analysis of Intensification, Extensification, and Decentralised Peripheral Densification

detail.title: Urban Transformation and Environmental Sustainability in Dhaka, Bangladesh: A Comparative Policy Analysis of Intensification, Extensification, and Decentralised Peripheral Densification

Acknowledgements: The author acknowledges urban planning researchers and practitioners across Bangladesh and South Asia whose field documentation underpins this analysis.

detail.abstract: Dhaka faces acute environmental stress driven by rapid population growth, speculative land conversion, and weak metropolitan governance. Between 1980 and 2022, more than 65 per cent of natural land cover was converted to impervious surface, intensifying flood risk, heat stress, air pollution, and the loss of ecological services. This article compares three urban growth pathways, Urban Intensification, Urban Extensification, and Decentralised Peripheral Densification, to identify the most environmentally sustainable and institutionally feasible strategy for Dhaka. The study combines qualitative policy analysis, secondary spatial and demographic evidence, comparative case material, and a weighted sustainability assessment across six indicators, complemented by institutional feasibility analysis. Urban Intensification scores 1.47 out of 3.00 and is constrained by green space loss, heat island amplification, and infrastructure overload. Urban Extensification performs worst at 1.10 out of 3.00 because of wetland destruction, biodiversity loss, and high service costs. Decentralised Peripheral Densification scores 2.88 out of 3.00 and performs best across five of six sustainability dimensions when supported by infrastructure sequencing, transit connectivity, and enforceable environmental standards. The findings indicate that Dhaka's most credible pathway is a polycentric metropolitan model anchored in transit connected sub centres, protected blue green infrastructure, and stronger metropolitan governance. The wider contribution of the article is a Dhaka specific comparative sustainability framework with relevance for rapidly growing South Asian megacities.

title: Monetary Policy Constraints in Russia amid the Pursuit of Technological Sovereignty: The Trade-off between Inflation and R&D Investment
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Monetary Policy Constraints in Russia amid the Pursuit of Technological Sovereignty: The Trade-off between Inflation and R&D Investment
detail.abstract: This paper examines the inherent conflict between the traditional objectives of Russian monetary policyprimarily inflation controland the strategic national goal of achieving technological sovereignty through increased investment in research and development (R&D). In an environment of structural sanctions, restricted access to foreign capital and technologies, and heightened macroeconomic volatility, the Bank of Russia faces a non-trivial trade-off. Restrictive monetary policy, while containing inflation, raises the cost of long-term borrowing and discourages R&D-intensive corporate investment. Conversely, accommodative policy to stimulate innovation risks de-anchoring inflation expectations. The research identifies the key transmission channels through which monetary tightening inhibits R&D spending, explores the limits of conventional policy instruments under technological autarky, and proposes a conceptual framework for balancing price stability with long-term innovative growth.

title: The Income-Wellbeing Nexus & The Ultimate Meaning of Happiness
affiliations: University of Girona - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Income-Wellbeing Nexus & The Ultimate Meaning of Happiness
detail.abstract: Using recent and robust data, we confirm a strong rank relationship between median disposable per-capita income and wellbeing at country level. Even so, a poor country may vastly improve wellbeing without pursuing economic growth; eventually, it will have to focus upon GDP to finance further wellbeing meliorations. Practically, when a country doubles per-capita income, a person gains 4 years of expected life at birth, 20 months of expected life at retirement and moves one up among 10 happiness bins. We compute bounds for these wellbeing markers at each income level to characterize what developmental policies may achieve when renouncing economic growth. We also list countries ranking better than expected on wellbeing, overachievers, as well as underachievers. Our code is 1-click reproducible.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission in the Era of High-tech Finance: New Channels and New Challenges
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Monetary Policy Transmission in the Era of High-tech Finance: New Channels and New Challenges
detail.abstract: This paper examines the transformation of the interest rate transmission mechanism under the conditions of rapid financial digitalization. The emergence of new financial intermediaries, decentralized finance (DeFi), digital lending platforms, and the growing role of big data and algorithmic pricing are reshaping how changes in the central bank policy rate affect the real economy. The research identifies novel transmission channels, including digital funding channels, crypto-asset price channels, and algorithmic expectation channels, while highlighting the risks of transmission fragmentation and uneven pass-through across sectors. The study concludes with policy recommendations for central banks to adapt their monetary policy strategies to the high-tech financial landscape.

detail.abstract: This research critically evaluates the systemic execution failures and financial inefficiencies within Pakistan's federal Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP). Utilizing an exploratory case study design and mixed-methods secondary data analysis, the study investigates the rapid degradation of public investment efficiency in the country. Quantitative findings reveal a staggering 59% project delay rate and an unsustainable "throw-forward" ratio frequently exceeding 10:1, which mathematically guarantees severe cost overruns and stretches theoretical completion times to an estimated 12 to 14 years. Concurrently, development expenditure has plummeted from historically high levels of 7.5% of GDP in the 1990s to approximately 1.0% today. Qualitative thematic analysis identifies political "pork-barrel" allocations, fundamental deficits in PC-1 planning frameworks (including optimism bias), erratic fund release mechanisms, and a lack of specialized project management human capital as the primary institutional root causes. The paper concludes that fixing the PSDP is an existential economic imperative, not merely an administrative challenge. Strategic recommendations include mandatory portfolio rationalization (scrapping non-performing projects), the imposition of statutory caps on new project approvals, integration with a Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF), and the professionalization of project leadership.

title: What does Income-conditioning Encode? A Decomposition of the Demographic-capital-flow Moderator

detail.title: What does Income-conditioning Encode? A Decomposition of the Demographic-capital-flow Moderator
detail.abstract: Since Peters (2025a), every paper in this series conditions demographic effects on per-capita income, entering Z₁ × log(GDP/capita) as the baseline moderator. Thirty-one papers embed this interaction; none have asked what institutional content it actually encodes. We decompose the interaction into five theory-imposed dimensions-social insurance (health and pension spending), financial depth, institutional quality, external credibility, and labor-market structure-and test whether the decomposition can replace or subsume the income moderator. Four pre-registered hypotheses all fail: the decomposition does not subsume the income interaction (H1), channels do not conform to theoretical predictions (H2), institutional dimensions do not collapse to low dimensionality post-residualization (H3), and the decomposition predicts subsample variation in Paper 18's coefficients worse than the simple income interaction (H4; MAPE 102.4 vs 70.9). The positive finding emerges from a residualized falsification (M8): two dimensions carry information beyond income itself. Social insurance-health and pension spending, operating on opposite signs for investment-survives on the savings, investment, and NFA channels across a 1970-2024 long-panel replication (N=950). Institutional quality (WGI-based) survives on the current-account channel, but only within Western Europe; a leave-one-region-out jackknife finds β(I₃) =-0.10 (ns) outside WEUR vs +1.31** in the full sample. Three dimensions-financial depth (r = 0.24 with log GDP/capita), external credibility, and labor-market structure (r = 0.81)-are statistically indistinguishable from income after residualization. A quadratic extension reveals that Z₁ × log(GDP/capita)² is additionally significant on current account (+3.97, p = 0.048) and NFA (+0.185, p = 0.011), suggesting residual nonlinearity in the income moderator that the series' linear specification does not capture. Series papers using Z₁ × log(GDP/capita) are not misspecified, but their coefficients aggregate three separable mechanisms: income level itself, social-insurance architecture, and (within Europe) institutional quality.

title: From Crude Exporter to Regional Refiner: Dangote Refinery and the Reconfiguration of West African Energy Trade
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Crude Exporter to Regional Refiner: Dangote Refinery and the Reconfiguration of West African Energy Trade
detail.abstract:
This paper studies whether the Dangote Refinery has begun to transform West Africa's position in the petroleum value chain. For two decades, Nigeria exported crude oil while importing most refined petroleum products, transferring refining margins abroad and leaving Nigeria and ECOWAS economies dependent on extra-regional fuel supply. Dangote's privately owned 650,000 barrel-per-day refinery creates the physical capacity to reverse that pattern. We ask whether this represents genuine structural upgrading or a shift toward what I call regionalized dependency: a regime in which external fuel dependence is reduced but regional supply becomes increasingly organized around a dominant Nigerian refining hub. 
We evaluate this question using three complementary empirical designs. First, a within-Nigeria product-level difference-indifferences design exploits the staggered rollout of Dangote's diesel and petrol production milestones. Using monthly NBS fuel-price data for 37 Nigerian states from 2017 to 2025, We find that the diesel-petrol price spread widened by NGN 568.5 per litre after the diesel milestone and narrowed by NGN 379.2 per litre after the petrol milestone. These symmetric product-specific responses provide the strongest evidence that the refinery's sequential rollout affected domestic retail price dynamics. Second, a PPML gravity model using UN Comtrade data from 2005 to 2024 finds no evidence of immediate export-led displacement of extra-regional refined-fuel suppliers: Nigeria's refined-product exports to ECOWAS remain 81 percent below the gravity benchmark in the first two post-Dangote years. Third, a Diebold-Yilmaz connectedness analysis using Bloomberg transport CPI indices shows that regional price connectedness rose from 8.6 percent before Dangote to 27.4 percent afterward, with Nigeria strengthening as a net price transmitter. 
Taken together, the evidence documents an early transition phase rather than a completed structural transformation. Dangote has created the capacity for regional energy reorganization, but the short post-treatment window and the simultaneous removal of fuel subsidies and liberalization of the Naira prevent a clean attribution of regional price leadership or trade-flow reconfiguration to the refinery alone.

title: Digital Infrastructure and the Spatial Allocation of Generation under Grid Constraints
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Infrastructure and the Spatial Allocation of Generation under Grid Constraints
detail.abstract:
Data centers now consume roughly 200 terawatt-hours of U.S. electricity annually, and demand is projected to double by 2030 as artificial intelligence workloads scale. This paper asks whether that concentrated load is reshaping the geography of electricity generation, not by slowing the grid connection process but by driving clean energy projects out of the interconnection queue in data-center-dense counties. 
Using a county-level panel covering the PJM Interconnection from 2015 to 2023, we combine project-level queue records with granular measures of data center employment to estimate an event-study design with county and year fixed effects. We test two hypotheses. First, we find no evidence that digital infrastructure exposure increases queue waiting times: estimated effects are small, statistically insignificant, and satisfy parallel trends, confirming that the administrative process is institutionally decoupled from local demand conditions. Second, we document a significant decline in queued generation capacity in high-exposure counties, concentrated at the tail of the data center distribution. A flow decomposition reveals that this decline is driven entirely by elevated withdrawal rates, projects enter the queue, discover high network upgrade costs through technical studies, and exit, while new entry rates are unaffected. Among the 47 most data-center-dense counties in the PJM footprint, clean energy withdrawals (solar, wind, and storage) increased by 6,846 MW between the pre-period (2015-2018) and post-period (2019-2023), compared with a 615 MW increase for fossil fuel projects. The interconnection queue functions as an information mechanism: it reveals the true cost of connecting in constrained locations, and developers respond by abandoning projects rather than building.

title: Capital Efficiency in U.S. AI Compute Infrastructure: A Strategic Determinant of National Competitiveness

detail.title: Capital Efficiency in U.S. AI Compute Infrastructure: A Strategic Determinant of National Competitiveness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is independent research, conducted without institutional affiliation or external funding, and the views expressed are the author's own. The analysis relies entirely on publicly available sources, including company filings, regulatory and market reports, and published research, all cited in the text; no proprietary or confidential data were used.

detail.abstract: The United States is financing the largest private infrastructure cycle in its history, with the five largest hyperscalers on course to spend on the order of $725 billion in 2026. This paper argues that the strategic variable is not the level of that spending but its efficiency, the capability generated per dollar of compute infrastructure. It develops a simple identity in which effective compute is the product of installed capacity, fleet utilization, model FLOPs utilization, and algorithmic efficiency, and shows that capability-per-dollar weights efficiency and unit cost symmetrically. Two results follow. A capex-equivalence rule prices a utilization gain in dollars of avoided investment: lifting fleet utilization from a 20% baseline to 35% frees more than 40% of the capital needed for a given capability. A parity condition shows when a smaller compute base can match a larger one, the formal shadow of the DeepSeek episode. Embedding an explicit compute scaling law shows that the concavity of capability in compute compresses even large compute gaps into much smaller capability gaps, the deeper reason efficiency, not only scale, is strategic. The paper documents the empirical landscape, the energy and financial channels through which efficiency becomes a national concern, and a set of disclosure, procurement, and energy-coupled policy instruments that would make capital efficiency measurable and rewarded.

title: The Dynamics of Fertility, Bargaining, and Human Capital Accumulation

detail.title: The Dynamics of Fertility, Bargaining, and Human Capital Accumulation
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of intrahousehold bargaining in shaping women's fertility decisions over the life cycle. I develop and estimate a quantitative life-cycle model featuring a dynamic feedback loop between fertility and bargaining power: childbirth lowers women's wages and outside options, weakening their bargaining position within the household and further constraining their autonomy over future fertility decisions. These bargaining concerns are quantitatively important in depressing marriage incentives, generating inefficient divorce, and consequently lower fertility at the household level. Exploiting the relaxation of the One-Child Policy in China, I show that couples with misaligned fertility preferences exhibit smaller fertility responses and higher divorce rates than couples with aligned preferences. The estimated model further indicates that such couples are less likely to form marriages and tend to marry at later ages. Removing bargaining frictions encourages earlier childbearing, increases completed fertility, and strengthens fertility response to family policies.

detail.abstract:
Background: While heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is one of the most common gynecological complaints in women, research on the impact of heavy menstrual bleeding is limited in low-middle income countries (LMICs). The goal of this study is to understand the experiences of women approaching or in perimenopause who endure HMB in rural Uganda.

Methods: Data from this cross-sectional study was collected as part of a larger cervical cancer screening study from May 2024 to October 2025 in rural Uganda. Women were eligible if they participated in the cervical cancer screening study and had menstruated in the past year. Participants were recruited door-to-door by village health teams. Participants completed an electronically administered baseline and endline survey about their demographics and menstrual health. Women were categorized as either HMB or light-moderate menstrual bleeding (LMMB). Counts and frequencies were reported.

Results: There were 121 women who reported having HMB, and 371 women LMMB. HMB participants were more likely to experience irregular and painful periods (p<0.001). They were also more likely to report that their period prevented them from carrying out work outside of the home (n=48, 39.7% HMB; n=50, 13.5% LMMB; p<0.001) and caring for their children (n=33, 27.3% HMB; n=37, 10% LMMB; p<0.001). Both groups reported a high level of comfort in seeking menstrual help r from a healthcare provider (n=117, 97.5% HMB; n=353, 95.4% LMMB; p=458). Finances were the biggest barrier for all participants in seeking help from a care provider.

Interpretation: There is a need for more research on the impact of menstruation on women in Uganda and similar LMICs. By better understanding the direct and indirect consequences of menstruation, we can develop practical support systems and policies for those impacted.

detail.abstract:
Background: Existing population-level surveillance of acute respiratory disease (ARD) hospitalizations – the most common reason for hospitalization among children – lack correlation with respiratory virus testing and forecasting. This retrospective cohort study models and forecasts pediatric ARD hospitalizations with seasonal patterns of respiratory viruses in Alberta, Canada.

Methods: From September 2010 to August 2025, all pediatric (age <18 years) ARD hospitalizations and respiratory virus tests in Alberta were identified in the Discharge Abstract Database (DAD) and Laboratory Information System (LIS), respectively. Traditional Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) models and those incorporating exogenous predictive variables (SARIMAX) (i.e., weekly percent positive tests for multiple respiratory viruses) were developed to forecast the outcome (i.e., weekly number of ARD hospitalizations). Models were developed for each ARD using backward elimination with data from September 2010 to August 2023. Forecast accuracy was evaluated against two years of data from September 2023 to August 2025 using a root mean square error (RMSE).

Findings: Over 15 years, there were 57,809 ARD hospitalizations: 17,613 (30·47%) bronchiolitis, 8,651 (14·96%) influenza-like illness, 15,759 (27·26%) pneumonia, 3,158 (5·46%) croup, 11,221 (19·41%) asthma exacerbations, and since March 2020 1,407 (2·43%) COVID-19. Compared with SARIMA models, SARIMAX models incorporating complex seasonal patterns of two or more co-circulating viruses produced more accurate forecasts of hospitalizations for each ARD as demonstrated by lower RMSE values.

Interpretation: SARIMAX models can be applied to existing ARD surveillance systems to accurately forecast the expected hospitalizations over the coming season. Equipping surveillance systems with real-time forecasts of clinical outcomes can inform public health and healthcare resource planning and preparedness.

title: Cardiometabolic Risk Phenotyping, Steatotic Liver Disease Burden, and Glycemic Control in Type 1 Diabetes from the MENA Region: A Multi-Center Population Based Study

detail.abstract:
Background: The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region carries the highest diabetes prevalence globally, at 17·6%, with an estimated 1·4 million individuals living with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D). Large-scale characterization of cardiometabolic risk, Steatotic liver disease, and microvascular complications in T1D from this region has not been reported.

Methods: This is a cohort study of 1,233 patients with T1D attending multi-center government endocrinology facilities in the UAE (EHR data: October 2025–February 2026). Comorbidities were ascertained from ICD-10 electronic records. Three pre-specified multivariable logistic regression models addressed three distinct clinical outcomes. Model-level goodness-of-fit (Nagelkerke R2, Hosmer–Lemeshow) and bootstrap-corrected AUROC for the composite cardiovascular score were additionally reported. Reporting follows the STROBE checklist.

Findings: Median age was 23 years (IQR 14–38); 51·6% were male; 38·1% were pediatric (<18 years). Median HbA1c was 9·1% (IQR 7·3–11·1); Approximately 76% of pediatric patients failed to achieve the ISPAD-recommended HbA1c target (≤7.0%), highlighting a substantial gap in glycemic control. ICD-coded MASLD was present in 3·5% of the cohort. Among adults with calculable FIB-4 (n=554), 10·5% had FIB-4 > 1·3 the AASLD threshold, warranting hepatological evaluation, including 2·9% with probable advanced fibrosis (FIB-4 >2·67). The composite cardiovascular risk score based on the multivariable logistic regression models yielded an AUROC of 0·883 (95% CI 0·849–0·917),which indicates good predictive performance of the cardiovascular risk score.Age (OR 1·06, 95% CI 1·039–1·082) and CKD/proteinuria (OR 4·15, 95% CI 1·898–9·068) were the dominant predictors of CVD. Dyslipidemia was the strongest predictor of microvascular complications (OR 2·50, 95% CI 1·712–3·643). CSII uptake was 6·9%.

Interpretation: This is the largest T1D cohort from the MENA region. The findings expose three clinically actionable service gaps: critically suboptimal glycemic control, undetected hepatic fibrosis in adults with T1D, and substantially under-recognized cardiovascular risk in adults under 45 years. National T1D registries, integrated hepato-endocrine care pathways, and expanded access to diabetes technology are warranted.

detail.abstract: This study examines the performance, sustainability, and effectiveness of Business Correspondents (BCs) in the Indian state of Odisha through a survey-based approach of both BCs and their customers. The study evaluates transaction patterns, income structures and institutional support of BCs, customer preferences and satisfaction levels. The findings reveal significant heterogeneity in BC performance across banks, with BCs affiliated with leading public sector banks outperforming those linked to other public and private sector banks in terms of transaction volumes, income stability, and customer trust. On the demand side, customers with higher age and located at a longer distance from bank branches exhibit a strong preference for BCs.

title: Regulatory Forbearance and Depositor Stickiness in Puerto Rico's Credit Union System: A Chronicle of Act 220-2015 and the Insolvency-Illiquidity Risk

detail.title: Regulatory Forbearance and Depositor Stickiness in Puerto Rico's Credit Union System: A Chronicle of Act 220-2015 and the Insolvency-Illiquidity Risk
detail.abstract: During 201318, Puerto Rico's locally chartered credit unions faced a crisis driven by their heavy concentration in government debt securities whose value collapsed alongside the island's fiscal position. Unrealized losses eventually exceeded the system's total indivisible capital, yet no systemic failure occurred. I argue that this outcome depended on the interaction of two mechanisms: a legislative accounting override that preserved reported solvency by deferring loss recognition, and the distinctive depositor loyalty rooted in the cooperative model's common-bond structure, which helped prevent the system-wide deposit light that would have forced bond liquidation at distressed prices. The contrast with the U.S. Savings and Loan experience is instructive: there, forbearance without comparable depositor stickiness proved insufficient

title: The Carney Doctrine: Canada’s Strategy for Navigating the Rupture

detail.title: The Carney Doctrine: Canada’s Strategy for Navigating the Rupture
detail.abstract: In the context of intensifying full-spectrum Great Power rivalry between the United States and China, Asia‑Pacific middle powers are confronted with pressures to make strategic choices in terms of alignment – “choose your patron”, in the words of one commentary. Their choices are necessarily constrained by geography, trade exposure, and security links.  Canada's revealed strategy – what might be labelled the Carney Doctrine for short – follows logically from three constraints that govern its policy choices: its status as a small open economy whose prosperity depends on a rules-based external environment; its geography, which favours north-south trade while exposing it to recurring bouts of U.S. expansionism and trade protectionism; and the economic and technological conditions of age of artificial intelligence as a factor of production (“machine knowledge capital”). The Carney Doctrine may usefully be parsed into three pillars that are consonant with these imperatives: support for a multilateral rules-based system (even if in rump form) coupled with trade and security diversification through middle-power networks; nation-building, including industrial policies that capitalize on Canada’s comparative advantages in the growth areas of the new age, including energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies; and above all the disciplined management of the continental relationship, which is best understood not as balancing between the superpowers but as sustaining a positive balance in a political-capital account with Washington while preserving “strategic autonomy”. There are two major Asia-Pacific elements embedded in this strategy. First, there is the “EU-CPTPP bridge”, which is explicitly referenced in the Carney Doctrine. Conceptually, this creates a caucus of small open economies stretching from the Pacific Rim through Canada to the European Union (which is a collection of small open economies) to enhance positive-sum economic cooperation while barring the weaponization of interdependence within the caucus. Second, while not explicitly stated in the Carney Doctrine, Canada has moved to normalize economic relations with China on more or less WTO terms even as it pivots to address the risks emanating from the United States. This normalization was accomplished through the respective visits of Prime Minister Mark Carney to Beijing in January 2026 and Foreign Minister Wang Yi to Ottawa in May 2026. In geopolitical terms, while conducted with less pomp and ceremony, these visits echo Richard Nixon’s visit to China in 1972 and the reciprocal visit of Deng Xiaoping to Washington in 1979, which normalized U.S.-China relations as the United States focussed on its geopolitical rivalry with the Soviet Union. In this note, I test the Carney Doctrine – so-stated – against three challenges: consistency with small-open-economy theory, robustness to the economic arithmetic imposed by economic geography; and viability in the face of a "realist" critique that can point to Washington’s reactions as reflected for example in the symbolic suspension of the Permanent Joint Board on Defence and thinly veiled threats from American commentators that echo the Athenian address to the Melians.

title: The Green Lerner Index
affiliations: and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Green Lerner Index
detail.abstract: This paper shows how climate externalities change antitrust targeting. We build a general-equilibrium oligopoly model with antitrust enforcement and greenhouse gas emissions. The central trade-off is that stronger competition reduces market-power distortions but can increase emissions by expanding output in polluting industries. We introduce a Green Lerner Index (GLI) that combines the private markup wedge with marginal climate damages and accounts for cross-sector reallocation. Calibrating the model with U.S. concentration, emissions, and output data, we show that the GLI ranking substantially changes enforcement priorities. Polluting industries become less attractive targets, while cleaner industries move up in the enforcement ranking. Our results show that emissions-adjusted targeting reduces the environmental cost of antitrust enforcement.

title: Human Behavioural Index (HBI): Constructing a Behavioural Composite Index from Digital Trace Data — Methodology and Preliminary Empirical Evidence

detail.title: Human Behavioural Index (HBI): Constructing a Behavioural Composite Index from Digital Trace Data — Methodology and Preliminary Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the Human Behavioural Index (HBI), a composite index constructed entirely from observable human behavioural signals — search query patterns, implied volatility data, social media engagement metrics, and news sentiment — rather than from market prices or returns. HBI aggregates seven theoretically grounded pillars — Attention, Fear and Anxiety, Herd Behaviour, Impulse, Social Validation, Desire and Aspiration, and Loyalty vs Switching — using a weighted z-score normalisation framework. The index is designed as a leading indicator of market sentiment, theoretically grounded in the observation that behavioural shifts precede economic decisions, which in turn drive market prices. 

This paper makes two contributions. First, it develops the full theoretical and mathematical specification of HBI, including pillar selection rationale, weight derivation, normalisation methodology, and a log-normal index construction model with composite-conditioned volatility scaling. Second, it provides preliminary empirical validation of the backtested implementation across 7,443 daily observations (January 2006 to May 2026), including descriptive statistics, pillar intercorrelation analysis, contemporaneous and lagged correlations with the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), predictive OLS regressions, and event-study analysis across three major macroeconomic events.

 Preliminary results indicate that the full HBI Score exhibits a contemporaneous correlation of 0.32 with VIX (p < 0.001). The Non-Fear HBI Component — which excludes the VIX-informed Fear pillar to test independent predictive power — exhibits a correlation of 0.13 with VIX (p < 0.001), suggesting that the non-VIX behavioural signals carry independent information about market stress. Predictive OLS regressions indicate that the Non-Fear HBI Component explains approximately 0.1% of VIX variance at a 5-trading-day horizon (p = 0.014). 

The paper acknowledges that the implementation presented is a proof-of-concept requiring full out-of-sample validation, peer review, and regulatory-grade data sourcing before HBI's leading indicator properties can be considered empirically established. These are identified as primary directions for future research.

title: The Apprenticeship Externality: AI and the Intertemporal Supply of Expertise

detail.title: The Apprenticeship Externality: AI and the Intertemporal Supply of Expertise
detail.abstract: Articial intelligence automates the routine, entry-level work through which professionals have long acquired judgment: verication skill was a by-product of doing generation tasks. We model this apprenticeship channel in a two-stage human-capital framework and show that automating generation erodes the steady-state supply of judgment. Because that judgment is largely general and verication confers benets beyond the rm, a training rm internalises only a share θ = (1-ρ)/(1 + ξ) < 1 of its value, which we micro-found in a labour market with poaching. A competitive market therefore over-automates the training ground and under-invests in deliberate training, both distortions springing from the same wedge. We call the cumulative shortfall expertise debtthe present value of foregone verication capacityand show that it is incurred now but repaid only over the slow horizon on which judgment accumulates, so that it is largely invisible at the point of decision. In general equilibrium the verication premium is a market price that rises as generation grows abundant; using AI to verify AI deepens the shortfall rather than relieving it; and a single subsidy to veried training, at rate (1/θ)-1 and largest in the most exposed professions, restores eciency. The framework provides a supply-side microfoundation for the verication constraint on AI's economic value.

title: Retail Order Flow: An Untapped Source of Alpha
affiliations: , Politecnico di Torino and Politecnico di Torino

detail.title: Retail Order Flow: An Untapped Source of Alpha
detail.abstract: Retail foreign-exchange (FX) order flow is widely dismissed as "noise." We argue the opposite: when retail trades are viewed through the right lens they embed a systematic, predictive signal that can be harvested. Using a body of academic work on retail biases, evidence from broker financial statements, expert interviews (n ~50) and proprietary trade-level data sets we postulate that: (i) unfiltered retail flow is reliably contrarian, exhibiting a persistent negative correlation with subsequent price moves; (ii) trades that embed both stop-loss and take-profit instructions concentrate information and accentuate this bias; and (iii) after a simple filter on realised revenue-per-million (RPM) the resulting "clean" flow delivers a forecastable edge that exceeds prevailing transaction costs. Across multiple independent lenses we converge on the same conclusion: retail order flow is an untapped source of exploitable alpha for proprietary desks and an effective hedge for brokers' dealing operations.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The United States small business sector — comprising over 33 million enterprises and accounting for 44% of national economic activity — faces a persistent and systemic credit gap estimated between $80 billion and $1.1 trillion annually. Traditional credit scoring models, built predominantly on historical financial data and FICO-based metrics, consistently fail to capture the true creditworthiness of small businesses, particularly those owned by minorities, women, and entrepreneurs in rural or underserved communities. This white paper presents a comprehensive, AI-powered Credit Risk Assessment Framework (AI-CRAF) specifically designed for small business lending in the United States. The proposed framework integrates traditional financial indicators with alternative data sources — including cash flow patterns, social media sentiment, online business reviews, supply chain relationships, and real-time payment histories — processed through advanced machine learning algorithms to generate dynamic, accurate, and bias-reduced credit risk scores.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The American Small Business Landscape Small businesses are definitively the engines of the American economy. According to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s 2023 Small Business Profile, firms with fewer than 500 employees account for 99.9% of all U.S. businesses, employ 46.4% of the private-sector workforce, and generate approximately 44% of U.S. GDP. In the decade from 2010 to 2020, small businesses created 10.5 million net new jobs, compared to 5.1 million for large enterprises. Yet access to capital — the lifeblood of business growth — remains profoundly unequal. The Federal Reserve’s 2023 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) found that 43% of small businesses experienced financial challenges in the prior 12 months. Among businesses that applied for financing, only 54% received the full amount requested.
declarations.funderStatement: Executive Summary: Small businesses represent the backbone of the American economy. With 33.2 million small businesses employing 61.7 million Americans — nearly half the private-sector workforce — their financial health directly impacts national economic stability, job creation, and innovation capacity. Yet, despite their enormous contribution, small businesses continue to face disproportionate barriers in accessing the capital they need to grow, innovate, and survive economic downturns. The core problem is structural: the credit assessment infrastructure currently serving U.S. small businesses was designed for a different era. Built on static, backward-looking financial data — tax returns, credit scores, collateral valuations — these traditional models systematically underestimate the creditworthiness of newer businesses, businesses with irregular revenue cycles, and businesses owned by individuals from historically marginalized communities. This paper proposes a solution: a nationally standardized, AI-powered Credit Risk Assessment Framework (AI-CRAF) that leverages the full breadth of data available in the digital economy — from real-time transaction data and cash flow analytics to social media sentiment, customer review scores, and supply chain health indicators.
