title: Seasonal Risk Preferences and the Market-Implied Response to Monetary Policy Path News
affiliations: State University of New York at New Paltz

detail.title: Seasonal Risk Preferences and the Market-Implied Response to Monetary Policy Path News
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether the financial-market response to Federal Reserve policy news depends on investors’ seasonal risk-bearing state. I combine daily Bekaert-Engstrom-Xu (BEX) measures of market-implied risk aversion and uncertainty with high-frequency Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) surprises and the daily Kamstra Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) onset/recovery measure. The evidence shows that near-term policy-path news, MP2, has seasonally state-dependent effects. In the preferred full asymmetric policy-news specification, dovish MP2 news lowers BEX risk aversion more strongly during onset states, when seasonal risk tolerance is deteriorating, while the corresponding uncertainty response is small and statistically insignificant. Risk-aversion-minus-uncertainty tests and residualized-risk-aversion diagnostics support the interpretation that the effect is concentrated in the market-implied price of risk. The result survives calendar, institutional, influence, randomization, and SAD phase-rotation robustness checks.

title: The Price of Long Hours
affiliations: KU Leuven, University of Antwerp and

detail.title: The Price of Long Hours
detail.abstract: Earnings premiums for long hours vary across occupations, shaping gender sorting and inequality. The leading explanation emphasizes firm-side production technologies, yet hours and wages are equilibrium outcomes reflecting worker preferences and market structure. We build a directed search-and-matching model that allows us to decompose the premium. Premiums compensate for the disutility of long hours and bargaining power; productivity explains little in Tech, where premiums approach 20%. This disutility is highest among women, who sort away from long-hours jobs; these amenity differences account for 22% of the gender earnings gap. In counterfactuals, general-equilibrium responses through market tightness substantially change policy impacts.

title: Navigating Change: Google Maps, Real-Time Information, and Transit Ridership
affiliations: , Deakin University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Navigating Change: Google Maps, Real-Time Information, and Transit Ridership
detail.abstract: Widespread adoption of smartphone applications has fundamentally changed how individuals navigate complex, information-rich environments. This paper examines how a key innovation in a ubiquitous smart phone app — Google Maps — has influenced travel behavior. Using a new dataset on the availability of real-time transit tracking within Google Maps across 128 transit systems, we show that ridership per capita was 14% greater three years after the staggered roll-out. Survey data on commutes confirms this pattern and shows that commuters substituted away from car trips. We see suggestive evidence that air quality improved. Google’s impact was largest in highly complex transit systems, and real-time tracking in alternative navigation applications had much smaller effects. Our findings highlight that cognitive costs are a crucial, but overlooked, determinant of urban travel.

title: Voter Preferences, Party Politics and Environmental Policy Reform
affiliations: , Vienna University of Economics and Business and Institut Mines-Télécom Business School

detail.title: Voter Preferences, Party Politics and Environmental Policy Reform
detail.abstract: Policymakers frequently implement environmental policies that are less ambitious than what voters would prefer. We document this gap using findings from previous research as well as evidence from climate policy in Austria's transport sector. To account for this pattern, we develop a model in which political parties compete with electoral platforms that involve multiple policy dimensions. When voters place greater weight on a primary issue -such as fiscal policy - than on environmental policy, we show that parties may refrain from proposing environmental reforms, even when these reforms enjoy broad public support. This dynamic arises once the primary issue becomes sufficiently salient to voters. We then examine potential ways to overcome this policy inertia, including the use of direct democratic instruments (e.g., referendums) and the delegation of environmental policy decisions from national to regional governments.

title: Congestion Pricing and Local PM2.5: Early Evidence from Fixed Monitors in New York City

detail.title: Congestion Pricing and Local PM2.5: Early Evidence from Fixed Monitors in New York City

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether implementation of New York City's congestion pricing program is associated with local changes in ambient PM2.5. I assemble a monitor-hour panel of fixed-site pollution readings across New York City and align each observation to New York local time, allowing treatment status and charged hours to match the program's legal geography and toll schedule. The empirical design compares treated and untreated monitors before and after implementation using difference-indifferences and triple-difference specifications with monitor, date, hour, and date-hour fixed effects, hourly weather controls, and small-cluster inference checks. Across specifications, PM2.5 declines more at legally treated monitors than at control monitors after the charge begins. The association is strongest under the baseline legal treatment definition, remains negative under a broader geographic treatment definition, and is more pronounced on weekdays and during charged hours. These patterns are robust to wildcluster bootstrap inference and are supported by placebo-assignment counterfactuals that randomly reassign treatment status across the monitor network. Event-study diagnostics, fakedate placebo tests, and donut-window checks further support the timing interpretation while also reinforcing the need for caution. The results do not estimate a full citywide causal effect, nor do they observe traffic volumes, route choices, or individual exposure. They provide early fixed-monitor evidence that implementation of the congestion charge is associated with a relative decline in local PM2.5 at monitored sites most directly tied to the policy's geography and timing.

title: Splitting the Price: Subscription Sharing and Monopoly Profits

detail.title: Splitting the Price: Subscription Sharing and Monopoly Profits

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have affected the redaction of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Agencia Estatal de Investigación (Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities), through grant PREP2023-001342, funded by MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033/ and by the FSE+. The grant is associated with the project PID2023-147136NB-100.

detail.abstract: I study whether subscription sharing raises monopoly profits. Sharing expands access for some consumers but cannibalizes individual subscriptions by replacing two accounts with one. I show that profitability depends on how consumers split the subscription price. I compare two price-sharing rules. Under equal sharing, partners split the price evenly. Sharing serves as a cost-reduction technology and is never profit-enhancing. Under proportional sharing, the pair pools valuations and subscribes whenever joint valuation exceeds the price. Sharing becomes profitable when sharing opportunities are sufficiently prevalent. Welfare effects are ambiguous because sharing expands access but raises optimal prices.

title: High School Class Scheduling and In-Class Work Production

detail.title: High School Class Scheduling and In-Class Work Production
detail.abstract: This study uses a reduced-form education production function framework to examine whether early or late period (edge-of-day) class scheduling predicts in-class academic work production and subsequent course outcomes. The setting is five Fall 2025 high school Geometry class sections taught by the same instructor. The analysis introduces EDGEDAY, a section-level weekly exposure index ranging from 0 to 10, with higher values indicating more frequent early-or late-day meetings. EDGEDAY separates observed student engagement level (ENCLASE) from completed mathematical work (PRACTICE). Across individual-level OLS, section-by-GPA group models, and student-week panel models, higher EDGEDAY exposure consistently predicts lower PRACTICE scores. The individual-level estimate is-0.109 (p = 0.007, N = 66). ASSESSMENT and PRECISE move in the same direction but are weaker downstream results, and PRECISE is interpreted cautiously because it partly incorporates PRACTICE. An exploratory IV/2SLS specification is retained in the appendix for transparency, but the weak first-stage diagnostic prevents a causal-identification claim. The contribution is local but concrete: schedule placement is associated with the classroom production environment. 1.

title: Bank Capital Shocks and Corporate Liquidity Policy: Evidence from India's Asset Quality Review (AQR)
affiliations: Goa Institute of Management, Indian Institute of Management Raipur and University of Connecticut - Department of Finance

detail.title: Bank Capital Shocks and Corporate Liquidity Policy: Evidence from India's Asset Quality Review (AQR)
detail.abstract: We examine how bank capital shocks affect corporate cash holdings using India's Asset Quality Review (AQR) as a regulatory shock to bank balance sheets. The AQR forced banks to recognize previously undisclosed non-performing assets and increase loan-loss provisions, leading to a staggered erosion of regulatory capital. Using bank–firm lending relationships and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that firms exposed to undercapitalized banks increase cash holdings by approximately 0.37% of total assets, or about 10% relative to pre-AQR levels. The effect is stronger among bank-dependent firms, firms with a higher likelihood of covenant violations, and firms borrowing from poorly capitalized banks. We further show that the marginal value of cash declines for exposed firms. These patterns are more consistent with an alignment motive than with a precautionary-savings explanation. Overall, bank capital shocks affect not only credit supply but also borrowers’ liquidity-management decisions.

title: Households’ Macroeconomic Beliefs: The Role of Education
affiliations: University of Padova, , Norges Bank and University of Padua

detail.title: Households’ Macroeconomic Beliefs: The Role of Education
detail.abstract: We design a novel survey to study how education shapes households' joint beliefs about inflation, unemployment, and monetary policy transmission. College-educated respondents perceive the inflation-unemployment trade-off and hold views similar to professional forecasters, while less educated respondents favor supply-side narratives. When exposed to hypothetical monetary policy interventions, the more educated update expectations and adjust consumption and saving in line with standard models, whereas the less educated display greater rigidity. This education gradient persists after controlling for information sources, financial literacy, and institutional trust, pointing to differences in abstract reasoning. Open-ended responses are consistent with college-educated households holding mental models aligned with standard macroeconomic theory.

title: Information-Sensitive Funding and Pre-Failure Flight
affiliations: Bradley University - Foster College of Business

detail.title: Information-Sensitive Funding and Pre-Failure Flight
detail.abstract: We ask whether US bank failures reflect asset-side insolvency or liability-side runs, arguing that both are projections of a single variable: the information sensitivity of the withdrawing creditor class. Extending Blickle, Brunnermeier, and Luck (2024) from the 1931 German crisis to US commercial-bank failures (1991–2022), we build five creditor classes from New York Fed Call Report data and measure pre-failure flight against size-matched controls. The three informed classes show 20, 44, and 49 percentage points of excess flight; the two uninformed classes show none. A Granger test finds asset deterioration leads wholesale flight, while uninsured-deposit flight leads asset markdowns—the within-bank signature of the 2023 SVB episode. A difference-in-differences analysis around the 2018 EGRRCPA increase in the SIFI threshold finds that treated banks lowered their equity ratio by 1.5 percentage points more than controls (p=0.041), consistent with a discrete easing of regulatory pressure on the treated banks.

title: Wage Penalty in the Hospitality Sector: Tips, Skills and Sorting
affiliations: and Nevin Economic Research Institute (NERI)

detail.title: Wage Penalty in the Hospitality Sector: Tips, Skills and Sorting
detail.abstract: Hospitality workers are among the lowest-paid employees in Europe. Whether this reflects differences in worker and firm characteristics or an additional sector-specific wage penalty remains an open question. This paper estimates the presence and magnitude of the penalty in Western Europe by comparing hospitality workers with a counterfactual group of workers employed in other sectors. Using matched employer-employee data and the reweighted decomposition, which adjusts for differences in the distribution of observable characteristics, we document a persistent unexplained wage gap of 5 to 15 percent per hour, on average, in most countries. The penalty widens across the wage distribution, with high-percentile earners facing the largest gap, indicative of a glass-ceiling pattern within the sector. Accounting for tips and bonuses does not narrow the gap but widens it, because bonuses in other sectors outweigh tips in hospitality. Finally, after controlling for field-of-study mismatch, we show that returns to education in the accommodation are not lower than in other comparable sectors.

title: The Hidden Cost of Going Public: Evidence from Employee Wellbeing
affiliations: Hanken School of Economics

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Going Public: Evidence from Employee Wellbeing
detail.abstract: How do IPOs affect employee wellbeing? Using a large panel of Glassdoor reviews and a difference-in-differences approach, we find that employee ratings decline significantly and persistently following IPO completion, particularly during the first two years after listing. The decline is substantially mitigated by labor union coverage and is concentrated among white-collar and low-tenure employees. Firms exposed to stronger post-IPO market scrutiny — such as higher stock sensitivity to earnings, a greater propensity to beat forecasts, VC backing, and greater analyst coverage — experience more pronounced declines. Textual analysis further reveals that employees express greater concerns about performance pressure and job insecurity after going public, particularly in firms facing higher market scrutiny. Together, the evidence suggests that heightened market scrutiny is a central channel through which public listing adversely affects employee wellbeing.

title: Bank valuation and macroprudential capital buffers
affiliations: De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: Bank valuation and macroprudential capital buffers
detail.abstract: How do unexpected changes in macroprudential capital buffer requirements impact bank valuation, measured by price-to-book ratios? This study addresses this question by constructing macroprudential capital buffer ”surprises” from market reactions to buffer announcements and estimating their effects, using panel local projections, on the price-to-book ratios of a panel of large European banks. The analysis shows that unexpected buffer surprises are associated with a short-run decline in price-to-book ratios, followed by a sustained increase in the weeks following the announcement. Such an increase is consistent with market recognition of reduced risk, despite higher buffer requirements that could lower distributable resources, suggesting that the risk channel dominates the payout channel in the valuation of large European banks.

title: CONCEPT NOTE -FOR DISCUSSION AND PEER REVIEW Consumer-Driven VAT Enforcement A Self-Governing Revenue Mobilisation Framework for Bangladesh

detail.title: CONCEPT NOTE -FOR DISCUSSION AND PEER REVIEW Consumer-Driven VAT Enforcement A Self-Governing Revenue Mobilisation Framework for Bangladesh

This study was conducted independently as a conceptual policy design framework for public discussion and peer review.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it is a conceptual policy design and theoretical framework that does not involve human subjects, patient data, or empirical field participants.

detail.abstract:
Bangladesh's tax-to-GDP ratio is among the lowest in the world, estimated at roughly 6.5-7.5% in recent fiscal years and reported by the World Bank at 8.2% as recently as 2024 depending on the measure and year used; NBR's own data showed the ratio falling to 6.56% in FY25 from 7.2% in FY24 [1]. Bangladesh's own Medium and Long-Term Revenue Strategy (2025-2035) targets raising this to 10.5% by FY35 [2], an explicit acknowledgement from NBR itself that current collection is far short of what the country needs. Despite legislative reform through the VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 (implemented 1 July 2019) [3], compliance at the retail and service level continues to be weak. Enforcement-led approaches have yielded limited returns, constrained by NBR capacity and the size of the informal economy.

The idea here is to shift VAT enforcement from the supply side to the demand side: give consumers a direct financial reason to demand proper VAT documentation at the point of sale. The mechanism pairs an instant cashback — funded through a real-time escrow that ringfences VAT the moment payment is made — with an annual tax rebate for registered taxpayers tied to verified VAT spending.

What follows is a concept note, not a feasibility study, and it is meant to be argued with. The cashback rate, the projected compliance uplift, the rebate cap, the rollout sequencing — these are working assumptions chosen to make the idea concrete enough to critique, not settled parameters. Several are flagged as untested where they appear. A fiscal microsimulation, a legal drafting review, and a capacity-building plan would all need to happen before anyone decided to pilot this; none of that work exists yet. Where the note leans on international examples, the citations are there so a reader can check them and push back.

Revised July 2026 (v1.2). This version adds a structural analysis of Dhaka Metropolitan Police's AI traffic enforcement system (launched April 2026) as a domestic proof of concept for the escrow mechanism's core design principle: that compliance improves when enforcement is automated at the moment of the event rather than delegated to a field officer's discretion. Earlier revision (v1.1, June 2026) substantially rewrote the problem statement with current IMF and World Bank citations, added detailed analysis of the 2021 NBR EFD lottery failure drawing on NBR's own documented admissions, and grounded the fiscal sustainability discussion in Bangladesh-specific data (NBR VATE assessment, BBS HIES 2022). Reference list expanded from 27 to 46 entries.

title: Interrelations between bitcoin market sentiment, crude oil, gold, and the stock market with bitcoin prices: Vision from the hedging market
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Glasgow and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Interrelations between bitcoin market sentiment, crude oil, gold, and the stock market with bitcoin prices: Vision from the hedging market

publicationDetails.detailsText: Studies in Economics and Finance, 41(5), 1166-1190. DOI:10.1108/SEF-03-2024-0137

detail.abstract:
Purpose
The purpose of this study is to examine Bitcoin's price behavior across market conditions, focusing on the influence of Bitcoin's historical prices, news sentiment and market indicators like oil prices, gold and the S&P index. The authors also assess the stability of Bitcoin-inclusive hedging portfolios under different market conditions, for example, bearish, bullish and moderate market states.

Design/methodology/approach
This study uses the Quantile Autoregressive Distributed Lag model to explore the effects of different factors on Bitcoin's prices across various market situations. This method allows for a detailed analysis of historical trends, investor expectations and external market influences on Bitcoin's price movements and systematic stability.

Findings
Key findings reveal historical prices and investor expectations significantly influence Bitcoin in all market scenarios, with news sentiment exhibiting substantial volatility. This study indicates that oil prices have minimal impacts on Bitcoin, whereas gold is a stabilizing asset in bear markets, with the S&P index influencing short-term fluctuations. At the same time, Bitcoin's volatility varies with market conditions, proving more efficient as a hedging tool in bear and stable markets than in bull ones.

Originality/value
This study highlights the intrinsic correlation between Bitcoin's prices, news sentiment and financial market indicators, enhancing understanding of Bitcoin's market dynamics. The authors demonstrate Bitcoin's weak direct correlation with commodities like oil, the stabilizing role of gold in crypto portfolios and the stock market's indirect effect on Bitcoin prices. By examining these factors' impacts across various market conditions, the findings offer strategies for investors to improve hedging and portfolio management in cryptocurrency markets.

The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1108/SEF-03-2024-0137

title: Intelligent Production Capacity and the New Geography of Value Evidence from the Chiba Bay Energy–Compute Corridor

detail.title: Intelligent Production Capacity and the New Geography of Value Evidence from the Chiba Bay Energy–Compute Corridor
detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, electrification, and digital infrastructure is reshaping the foundations of economic geography. This paper proposes the Energy–Compute–Real Estate–Finance (EREF) Framework to explain how regions possessing abundant electricity, extra-high-voltage (EHV) grid access, and conversion-ready industrial assets may gain structural advantages in the emerging Intelligence Flow era.

At the center of the framework is Intelligent Production Capacity (IPC), defined as a territory’s ability to transform electricity into economic intelligence and intelligent production value through compute infrastructure, physical assets, and financial scaling mechanisms.

Using the Chiba Bay Energy–Compute Corridor as a case study, the paper demonstrates how Futtsu, Kimitsu, and Kisarazu—collectively referred to in this paper as the Greater Mitsu District (三津地区)—form an integrated energy–compute production core, while Urayasu functions as an ultra-low-latency metropolitan interface to Tokyo. This spatial configuration illustrates how legacy industrial districts may be revalued as strategic digital infrastructure platforms.

The paper makes three contributions: it formalizes the concept of Intelligent Production Capacity (IPC), develops the five-layer EREF Stack, and presents the first spatial model of the Chiba Bay Energy–Compute Corridor. More broadly, the framework provides a new analytical lens for understanding asset repricing, infrastructure transformation, and the evolving geography of economic value in the AI era.

title: The impact of renewable energy on extreme volatility in wholesale electricity prices: Evidence from organisation for economic co-operation and development countries
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: The impact of renewable energy on extreme volatility in wholesale electricity prices: Evidence from organisation for economic co-operation and development countries
detail.abstract:
As global climate change intensifies, the Paris Agreement aims to limit global temperature increases to within 2 • C above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 • C. A key strategy to achieve this goal is accelerating the transition of the power grid to renewable energy sources. This study uses annual data and constructs annual extreme positive and negative wholesale electricity price fluctuations from daily weighted wholesale electricity spot prices. It examines the impact of various renewable energy sources on extreme positive and negative wholesale electricity price fluctuations in 32 Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development countries from 2015 to 2023. Using dynamic panel threshold regression, we find that the proportion of renewable energy generation significantly reduces extreme price fluctuations once certain thresholds are exceeded. This finding underscores the importance of developing renewable energy sources such as hydropower, wind power, solar power, and biomass energy. It also highlights the challenges posed by the intermittency and unpredictability of renewable energy at lower penetration levels. Policy recommendations include developing energy storage technologies, building modern grid infrastructure, and formulating policy incentives to support the diversification of renewable energy. Future research should focus on the long-term impacts of renewable energy integration and the role of policy frameworks in supporting this transition, ensuring a comprehensive and sustainable energy transformation. The full paper is available at:

 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2024.144343

title: Assessing the Influences of Livelihood Support Under Tanzania’s Productive Social Safety Net on Household Food Insecurity among Beneficiary Households
affiliations: Sokoine University of Agriculture, Sokoine University of Agriculture and Sokoine University of Agriculture

detail.title: Assessing the Influences of Livelihood Support Under Tanzania’s Productive Social Safety Net on Household Food Insecurity among Beneficiary Households
detail.abstract: Food insecurity continues to affect many poor and vulnerable households in Tanzania despite ongoing investments in social protection programmes. This study examined whether livelihood support interventions provided through the Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN) programme contribute to improved household food security. The analysis covered four councils in Tanzania and employed a quasi-experimental design using Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATET) approach. Primary data were collected from 400 PSSN beneficiary households, including 160 households that received both cash transfers and livelihood support interventions and 240 households that received cash transfers only. Household food insecurity was assessed using the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS). The matching procedure improved comparability between treatment and control households by reducing differences in observable characteristics. The results showed that households receiving livelihood support recorded a lower average HFIAS score (9.26) than households receiving cash transfers only (10.21). The estimated ATET coefficient (-0.95) indicated lower food insecurity among livelihood support beneficiaries. However, the estimated effect was not statistically significant (p = 0.466). These results suggest that although livelihood support may contribute to better food security outcomes, the observed improvement was not large enough to demonstrate a measurable programme effect during the study period. The study recommends strengthening productive inclusion through improved access to credit, productive assets, market opportunities, and complementary support services to enhance the effectiveness of livelihood support interventions and promote sustainable food security outcomes.

title: News sentiment, climate conditions, and New Zealand electricity market: A real-time bidding policy perspective
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: News sentiment, climate conditions, and New Zealand electricity market: A real-time bidding policy perspective
detail.abstract: We investigate the short-and long-term dynamics between news sentiment, climate conditions, and New Zealand's wholesale electricity prices. Remarkably, our analysis is mainly grounded in investigating and comparing the determinants of power before and after implementing the real-time bidding policy in New Zealand. We apply the Quantile Autoregressive Distributed Lag (QARDL) approach to address the complex nature of these indicators effectively. Specifically, before implementing the real-time bidding policy, the electricity prices presented salient asymmetry and a non-linear structure in response to climate conditions, news sentiment, and consumer demand, consolidating the market's sensitivity to exogenous conditions in the short and long run. Interestingly, the realtime bidding shock substantially altered these powers, mainly manifested by the stylized fact that the market's response to these factors became noticeably more stable. Further, the market's ability to absorb price fluctuations is also significantly strengthened in the long term due to the insensitive response of the electricity market to climate conditions. Our analysis also confirmed the solid relationship after the relevant policy introduction. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2025.134784

title: When Co-resident Pension Income Disappears: Labor Supply Responses in Multigenerational Households

detail.title: When Co-resident Pension Income Disappears: Labor Supply Responses in Multigenerational Households
detail.abstract: In middle-income countries a public pension often supports not just a retiree but an entire multigenerational household. What happens to that family when the retired elder leaves and the pension income disappears? The question has gone largely unexamined. Using a rotating panel of Brazilian households, I follow the families of co-resident retired elders who exit during the survey. When no new members move in, total household income falls by about 44 percent, close to the full pension, while income per person stays roughly flat as the household shrinks. The remaining working-age members raise their labor force participation by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points, an adjustment borne mainly by the retiree's adult children, whom survivor-pension rules leave uncovered. In the same families, enrollment in the Bolsa Família cash-transfer program rises by 4.6 percentage points. Public pensions in aging middle-income economies insure households, not only their nominal beneficiaries.

title: Grade2Stage: Grade-driven pT Stage Prediction in Whole Slide Images of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
affiliations: Korea University, Korea University, The Catholic University of Korea, Gachon University and Korea University

detail.title: Grade2Stage: Grade-driven pT Stage Prediction in Whole Slide Images of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
detail.abstract: The increasing clinical demand for accurate cancer staging highlights the need for robust computational methods in digital pathology. In particular, predicting the pathological T (pT) stage from whole slide images (WSIs) requires precise modeling of both local morphological characteristics and global context information. While recent deep learning approaches have achieved notable progress in WSI-level prediction, many rely solely on visual features and overlook critical semantic cues such as nuclear grade that are strongly associated with tumor aggressiveness and progression. In this paper, we present Grade2Stage, a novel grade-driven framework for pT stage prediction in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Our method integrates patch-level grade features through two complementary branches: a graph neural network branch that models spatial relationships among patches using grade features, and a convolutional neural network branch that processes patch-level grade predictions. The features from both branches are fused into a unified representation for final pT stage classification. We evaluate our method on two datasets: the publicly available TCGA-KIRC and a private in-house cohort. Experimental results demonstrate that Grade2Stage achieves competitive performance and consistently improves over conventional baselines in several settings, highlighting the benefit of incorporating grade-aware information into WSI-based staging.

title: The Economic Benefits and Costs of AI and Policies to Mitigate AI's Impact on Inequality
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics and University of Glasgow

detail.title: The Economic Benefits and Costs of AI and Policies to Mitigate AI's Impact on Inequality
detail.abstract: We examine the economic impact of increasingly productive AI and policies that spread its benefits across the economy. Improvements in AI productivity trigger labor reallocation and changes in absolute and relative wages for different types of labor. Wages of labor that is essential for building AI increase faster than overall GDP. Wages of labor that is substituted for by AI decrease in both absolute and relative terms. Wages of labor that is used only in final goods production and is not displaced by AI increase in line with overall GDP. We contrast the impact of productivity gains depending on whether AI production is competitive or monopolistic. Monopoly production of AI restricts its deployment, slowing the transition and impact of AI. Optimal tax and regulatory policies that achieve Pareto-improvements differ depending on whether there is competition in AI production.

title: Adjudication Holds on Benefit Requests Implicated in Presidential Proclamations 10949 and 10998

detail.title: Adjudication Holds on Benefit Requests Implicated in Presidential Proclamations 10949 and 10998

publicationDetails.detailsText: St. Louis Law Journal, Volume 3, Issue 1, Pp. 22-23

detail.abstract:
This article examines the legal and practical implications of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Policy Memorandum PM-602-0194, which imposed adjudicative holds on immigration benefit requests associated with Presidential Proclamations 10949 and 10998. The article analyzes how these executive actions expanded restrictions on nationals from designated countries beyond admission into the United States by indefinitely delaying the adjudication of immigration benefit applications, including adjustment of status, employment authorization, and extensions of lawful status.

The article further explores the emerging judicial response to these policies through an analysis of Saghafi v. Edlow and Doe v. Trump, where federal district courts concluded that USCIS's blanket adjudicative hold policy likely conflicts with Congress's statutory mandate requiring the agency to adjudicate immigration benefit applications. By examining the interaction between executive authority, administrative agency discretion, and congressional directives, the article argues that these decisions establish meaningful limits on USCIS's ability to suspend adjudications indefinitely through internal policy memoranda. Finally, the article discusses the practical consequences of these policies for immigration practitioners and affected applicants while considering the broader implications for administrative law, judicial review, and the future of immigration adjudications.

title: Reliability-aware transformer-to-CNN knowledge distillation for efficient cotton leaf disease classification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Reliability-aware transformer-to-CNN knowledge distillation for efficient cotton leaf disease classification
detail.abstract: Early and accurate detection of cotton leaf diseases is crucial for reducing yield loss, protecting fiber quality, and supporting effective crop management. Although deep learning models demonstrate strong performance in plant disease classification, many high-performing methods are computationally demanding and lack sufficient evaluation for prediction reliability. In this study, we propose a heterogeneous knowledge distillation framework for cotton leaf disease classification, employing a Swin-Small transformer as the teacher model and EfficientNetV2-S and DenseNet121 as student models. Experiments were performed on a five-class cotton leaf dataset containing 1,373 images. The dataset was divided into an 80% cross-validation pool, a 10% calibration set, and a 10% independent test set. Five-fold cross-validation was performed, followed by temperature scaling and conformal prediction to improve prediction reliability. Among all evaluated models, the distilled Swin-Small to EfficientNetV2-S model demonstrated the best fold-wise performance, yielding 95.22 ± 0.58% accuracy, 95.46 ± 0.51% precision, 95.21 ± 0.59% F1-score, and 99.24 ± 0.21% AUC. Compared with the standalone EfficientNetV2-S model, knowledge distillation improved test accuracy from 92.03% to 95.22%, resulting in a gain of 3.19 percentage points. Its calibrated five-fold ensemble achieved 95.65% accuracy, 96.07% precision, 95.67% F1-score, and 99.38% AUC, outperforming all standalone baselines. The distilled Swin-Small to DenseNet121 model achieved 94.93 ± 1.21% accuracy with only 6.96M parameters. Additionally, temperature scaling reduced the expected calibration error from 0.0365 to 0.0248. These results demonstrate that transformer-to-CNN knowledge distillation can improve classification performance, model reliability, and practical deployment potential in cotton disease diagnosis.

title: Territorial inequality in oncology clinical trial participation and cancer mortality in Spain: a longitudinal ecological study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hospital General Universitario de Elche, University of Murcia - Virgen de la Arrixaca University Clinical Hospital, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Lausanne - Lausanne University Hospital, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hospital Clinico San Carlos - Department of Medical Oncology

detail.title: Territorial inequality in oncology clinical trial participation and cancer mortality in Spain: a longitudinal ecological study
detail.abstract: Background: In Spain, universal coverage is delivered through 17 decentralised Autonomous Communities. We quantified territorial inequality in oncology clinical trial-participation density and examined its ecological association with age-standardised cancer mortality.Methods: We used a longitudinal ecological design with regions as the unit of analysis. Trial-participation density (participants per 100,000 population, 2016-2020) and annual authorised oncology trial counts (2015-2022) came from the Spanish Registry of Clinical Studies. Annual age-standardised cancer mortality came from the Spanish National Statistics Institute. Inequality was described with means, standard deviations, ranges, coefficients of variation, and maximum/minimum ratios. The main analysis used repeated-measures ecological models with calendar-year indicators and region-clustered standard errors, with sensitivity analyses for ageing, population weighting, GDP, post-exposure years, influence, HC3 errors, and wild cluster bootstrap inference.Results: Trial-participation density varied from 0.2 to 41.9 per 100,000 population (mean 15.0, SD 10.5; coefficient of variation 70.2%), a 209-fold regional difference. Mean cancer mortality excluding 2020-2021 varied less (mean 231.5, SD 11.7 per 100,000; coefficient of variation 5.1%). Mean mortality declined from 245.5 per 100,000 in 2015 to 216.5 in 2024. In the year-adjusted repeated-measures model, a 10-unit increase in trial-participation density was associated with -6.6 fewer cancer deaths per 100,000 (95% CI -12.0 to -1.3), equivalent to moving from the lowest to the median regional participation level. After ageing adjustment, the estimate was -5.5 (95% CI -10.3 to -0.7) per 10-unit increase. The post-exposure 2022-2024 analysis preserved the direction and similar magnitude of the association. Population weighting preserved the association, and GDP total attenuated it.Conclusions: In Spain, oncology trial participation is geographically concentrated. Regions with higher trial-participation density had persistently lower ecological cancer mortality, although the association is closely linked with metropolitan scale and oncology-system capacity. Trial infrastructure should be treated as a cancer-equity issue; causal interpretation requires finer geographic and patient-level data.

title: Compute as a Hedgeable Production Input: Financial Reporting, Risk Management, and Valuation Implications of Compute Capacity Futures

detail.title: Compute as a Hedgeable Production Input: Financial Reporting, Risk Management, and Valuation Implications of Compute Capacity Futures
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is commonly described as software because its outputs are digital and its revenues are often subscription-based. Economically, however, generative AI production depends on a constrained, price-sensitive, energy-intensive, and increasingly benchmarked input: compute capacity. The planned emergence of compute futures, GPU rental-rate indices, and forward curves creates a new reporting and valuation problem. Once compute becomes observable, forward-priced, and potentially hedgeable, it can no longer be treated merely as an opaque cloud expense buried inside broad infrastructure or cost-of-revenue pools.

This paper develops an integrated financial reporting, risk management, and valuation analysis of compute capacity futures and related AI infrastructure arrangements under IFRS, US GAAP, and Brazilian CPC. It distinguishes cash-settled derivatives, own-use and normal-purchase procurement contracts, embedded derivatives, dedicated-capacity arrangements, leases, take-or-pay commitments, hedge-accounting relationships, and onerous-contract indicators. The accounting treatment of any specific arrangement depends on contract specifications, settlement mechanics, benchmark methodology, intended use, contractual rights and obligations, hedge designation, and entity-specific facts and circumstances.

The paper introduces Computational Capacity Risk, Compute Cost-at-Risk, Hedge-Adjusted Compute Cost, Hedge-Adjusted Algorithmic Contribution Margin, technical basis risk diagnostics, and Compute Beta as analytical tools for preparers, auditors, CFOs, boards, investors, valuation professionals, and standard-setters. These measures are not proposed as official accounting categories. They are designed to translate compute exposure from an operational procurement issue into a financial reporting, treasury, governance, and asset-pricing problem.

The central implication is that AI companies should not receive software-style valuation treatment merely because their products are digital. Where revenue depends on volatile and potentially hedgeable compute inputs, investors and auditors need to evaluate margin resilience, hedgeability, benchmark quality, disclosure discipline, and the economic substance of algorithmic production.

title: Schrödinger’s Chatbot: Platform Liability, Volition, and Generative AI
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast - School of Law

detail.title: Schrödinger’s Chatbot: Platform Liability, Volition, and Generative AI
detail.abstract:
Schrödinger's cat, sealed in its box, is simultaneously alive and dead—neither state actual until the moment of observation collapses the uncertainty into one outcome. A large language model, before any prompt is issued, presents an exact structural analogue: every prospective output sits, from the provider's vantage point, in a superposition of lawful and unlawful, collapsing only when the user's purpose materialises at the point of use. It may become quotation, criticism, parody, research, news-related use, private study, synthetic reformulation, or infringement. Its legal character materialises only when a user supplies the target, purpose, context and extent of the requested output.  A provider-primary liability rule forces the provider to act as though that collapse had already occurred—pre-clearing or blocking outputs whose legal character is unknowable without the context the user alone supplies. Lacking that context, the provider cannot invoke purpose-dependent exceptions and privileged uses; every arguable overlap must be treated as potentially infringing; and the result is systematic overblocking, multiplying veto points, and inflating transaction costs across the entire space of human knowledge the model has learned from.

This article calls that structural defect the Schrödinger's-chatbot problem, and its governing thesis is that collapse occurs at the point of use, not at the point of design. The argument operates across three connected layers. At the training stage, the article argues that learning is not, as such, reproduction. Model parameters encode statistical regularities, not recognisable protected expression recoverable from the trained artefact; ancillary technical copies in the training workflow must be assessed through the ordinary text-and-data-mining and temporary-copying architecture, but the model itself should not be treated as a copy of its corpus. At the output layer, the article argues that rights-relevant reproduction or communication, where it occurs at all, is ordinarily attributable to the user’s volitional act: the prompt that selects the object, purpose and form of the use. Provider responsibility re-enters not through strict or primary liability for every user-prompted output, but through fault-sensitive doctrines: active role, inducement, systematic steering toward infringing outputs, knowledge of identifiable unlawful outputs, business-model dependence on substitution, or failure to adopt proportionate safeguards against known extraction patterns.

Like Company v Google Ireland Limited (Case C-250/25), the first CJEU preliminary reference on generative AI and copyright, GEMA v OpenAI, Getty Images v Stability AI, Bartz v Anthropic, Thomson Reuters v Ross Intelligence and pending US music and news litigation are used throughout the article as litigation signals placed at the doctrinal pressure points they illuminate. The Article connects copyright doctrine to intermediary liability, fundamental-rights proportionality, law-and-economics, and platform governance. The proposed framework is not a plea for immunity. It supports notice-and-action, targeted injunctions, guardrails, auditability, transparency and role-split remedies. Nor does it deny the remuneration gap. It argues instead that creator compensation should be addressed candidly through a liability-rule mechanism—a permitted-but-paid statutory remuneration right where commercial systems extract systematic value or produce demonstrable substitution—rather than by mischaracterising learning as copying or the provider as the author of every output. Copyright should protect expression and sustain creative labour without enclosing learning, suppressing lawful uses, or turning general-purpose cultural tools into machines of anticipatory censorship.

title: FinSentiment Alpha: NLP-Based Sentiment Signals for Long-Short Equity Strategies in US Markets Working Paper

detail.title: FinSentiment Alpha: NLP-Based Sentiment Signals for Long-Short Equity Strategies in US Markets Working Paper
detail.abstract: I examine whether transformer-based sentiment signals extracted from mandatory SEC filings contain exploitable alpha in US equity markets. Using Fin-BERT, a domain-adapted BERT model pre-trained on financial text, I score the Management Discussion and Analysis sections of 863 10-K and 10-Q filings from 45 large-cap US firms over April 2019 through November 2023. At each monthly rebalancing date, I sort firms into quintiles based on the change in their sentiment score since the prior filing, go long the most improved quintile, and short the most deteriorated quintile. A mandatory 3-day publication lag eliminates look-ahead bias and a 2 basis point per-leg transaction cost is applied throughout. Under walk-forward validation across four folds, the strategy produces an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.054 and annualized return of 17.67% with a maximum drawdown of-9.38%. In-sample Sharpe is 1.075, suggesting limited overfitting across the validation folds. These results indicate that qualitative disclosures in regulatory filings contain cross-sectionally predictive information not fully captured by traditional price-based factor models, and complement recent work applying large language models to formulaic alpha discovery on Chinese equity markets [Yu et al., 2026].

title:
The Impact of Organizational Justice on Public Service Motivation and Turnover Intentions:
 An Empirical Analysis within German Local Government Administration
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Impact of Organizational Justice on Public Service Motivation and Turnover Intentions:
 An Empirical Analysis within German Local Government Administration
detail.abstract:
Public administrations, confronted with demographic change and intensifying competition for talent, face the dual challenge of sustaining employee motivation while securing long-term retention. This study investigates the role of organizational justice (OJ) in shaping Public Service Motivation (PSM) and turnover intention (TI) among employees in German municipal administrations. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), OJ is conceptualized not only as a resource but as an enabling condition for the effectiveness of PSM.

Cross-sectional survey data from 308 municipal employees were analyzed using validated scales and multivariate techniques, including regression and moderation analysis. Results indicate that distributive justice significantly predicts political motivation (Attraction to Policy-Making), while interactional justice is positively associated with altruistic orientations such as self-sacrifice. Procedural and distributive justice jointly emerge as strong negative predictors of turnover intention. Moderation analysis further demonstrates that the protective effect of PSM against TI materializes only under conditions of high perceived fairness.

These findings reposition OJ from a normative principle to a strategic lever of HR management and governance. While the cross-sectional design and local sample limit generalizability, the study provides actionable insights for justice-sensitive HR strategies. Future research should employ longitudinal and cross-national designs to assess the durability and cultural specificity of these dynamics. In sum, the study advances theory-driven discourse on justice-based motivation and retention and outlines a pathway toward justice-based public governance.

title: How Does Product Market Competition Affect Disclosure of Management Forecasts? Evidence From China Imports
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Accounting and

detail.title: How Does Product Market Competition Affect Disclosure of Management Forecasts? Evidence From China Imports
detail.abstract: Prior research investigates the relation between product market competition and management forecast decisions under the proprietary cost framework. We reexamine this relation through information demand and uncertainty channels, using Chinese imports as a largely exogenous measure of competition. We hypothesize that competition alters the intertemporal nature of management forecasts by raising investor and analyst demand for information about firms’ performance, especially short-term performance, while making it more difficult for managers to provide accurate long-horizon forecasts. Consistent with our predictions, competition increases the issuance of short-horizon forecasts, particularly for firms with greater information demand or higher uncertainty. Conversely, competition decreases the issuance of long-horizon forecasts, with this effect attenuated by information demand but amplified by uncertainty. Additional analyses indicate that our results are inconsistent with alternative explanations based on proprietary costs, outsourcing to China, expectation management, or bad-news hoarding. Our study offers new insights into how competition influences management forecast decisions.

title: From Rural Villages to Global Markets: Policy Lessons from China's Taobao Villages for Digital Finance Transformation
affiliations: University of Saskatchewan - Johnson-Shoyama Graduate School of Public Policy and University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM) - Université du Québec à Montréal

detail.title: From Rural Villages to Global Markets: Policy Lessons from China's Taobao Villages for Digital Finance Transformation
detail.abstract:
This paper was originally published as a policy brief in the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI) Future of Digital Finance series (September 2025). The version posted here is the published version.

Financial exclusion remains a significant barrier to inclusive economic development, particularly in rural regions where infrastructure gaps, limited access to credit, and low financial literacy constrain participation in formal financial systems. This policy brief examines China's Taobao Village model as an example of how digital platforms, public investment, and grassroots entrepreneurship can collectively expand financial inclusion and support rural economic transformation. Drawing on the experience of more than 7,700 Taobao Villages across China, the analysis highlights how integrated digital ecosystems can overcome traditional barriers to finance, commerce, and market access.

A central innovation of the model is the use of transaction and platform-generated data as a form of digital collateral, enabling automated credit assessment for small enterprises that lack conventional credit histories or physical collateral. Through the integration of e-commerce platforms, digital payments, logistics networks, and data-driven lending, the model has unlocked financing opportunities for millions of previously underserved entrepreneurs while supporting participation in national and global markets.

The brief argues that the value of the Taobao Village experience lies not in direct replication but in adapting its underlying principles to local contexts. These include building open and interoperable digital infrastructure, establishing trustworthy data governance frameworks, investing in human capital and digital literacy, and embedding equity considerations into digital transformation strategies. Drawing lessons for policymakers in emerging and developing economies, the brief proposes a framework for leveraging digital finance as a catalyst for inclusive growth while safeguarding competition, transparency, and social inclusion.

title: Corruption Control in Ancient India
affiliations: Punjab Agricultural University, LRM DAV College and Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana

detail.title: Corruption Control in Ancient India
detail.abstract: In the modern materialistic world corruption is rampant and leaders of organisations and state use all sorts of unfair means to make money. Despite several provisions against corruption, making money through unlawful practices goes on. One is curious to know about how the things have been managed in the past. Were the leaders of the grand ‘golden' ancient days less likely to succumb to temptations of public funds as compared to their counterparts in present times? This paper presents the principles and practices of making wealth and means of dealing with wrongdoers in ancient India. Key Words: Corruption, money, wealth, ethics, punishment for corrupt practices.

title: ConteX Law: The Conditional Law of Generative Determinism: A Theoretical Framework and Its Governing Law

detail.title: ConteX Law: The Conditional Law of Generative Determinism: A Theoretical Framework and Its Governing Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of SnapStak.ai, which develops the CON10X framework and CON10X 4N6 forensic pipeline described in this paper. The ConteX Law framework and the systems demonstrating it are the author's own intellectual property.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper sets out ConteX Law: the stated, reproducible relationship that governs whether a generative AI model produces a deterministic, accurate result or an unreliable, confabulated one. The central proposition is that accuracy is not a property of the model, its scale, or its compute, but a property of the structure imposed on the input. ConteX Law expresses this as a conditional: where the four governing pillars-Structure, Behaviour, Influence, and Objective-are satisfied to completeness for a given task, the model's capacity to confabulate collapses and its output becomes reproducible. The law is presented here in conditional form, the conditions under which it holds are defined, and the criteria by which it qualifies as a law-reproducibility, falsifiability, and model-independence-are examined against direct evidence. The conditional follows deductively once the four pillars are exhaustive, so the law is provable given a single falsifiable premise. The CON10X Web Domain provides that evidence: a documented result in which output was reproduced identically more than three hundred consecutive times under satisfaction of the four pillars. This paper describes what the law is, why it holds, and how the completeness gate that decides it is computed, set out in full so the relationship can be studied and reproduced.

title: Territorial Logic and its Limits: Re-reading Mahan, Mackinder, Spykman, and Brzezinski under Flow Conditions

detail.title: Territorial Logic and its Limits: Re-reading Mahan, Mackinder, Spykman, and Brzezinski under Flow Conditions

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the category system of the classical Anglo-American geopolitical tradition articulated across the 107-year arc from Mahan (1890) through Mackinder (1904), Spykman (1942-44), and Brzezinski (1997) and analyzes where its territorial assumptions reach their limits under the technological and civilizational conditions of the early twenty-first century. The argument is not a critique of the four authors, each of whom was a precise observer of his own era's strategic configuration. It concerns the category system itself, and the conditions under which its territorial logic ceases to capture the dynamics of contemporary global power.
The paper proceeds in six sections. Section II reviews the four classical authors as a coherent analytical
lineage with a single 107-year arc. Section III traces the two-hundred-year Great Game continuity from
the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) to the present, with the Crimean peninsula's threefold strategic role as
the structural marker connecting the classical phase, the Cold War, and the 2014-2026 transition. Section
IV examines where the tradition's core categories — territorial logic, national-state primacy, the
polis-state mediation layer, classical realpolitik — reach their structural limits.

Section V develops a flow-architectural reading as an analytical alternative, set beside the classical
categories rather than declared their successor: flow as foundational unit (with Mahan's proto-flow
priority), the four flow layers (raw-material and energy, commodity, information, financial), vortex
dynamics, time-compression, response-time and calibrated predictive capacity,
nodes-hubs-redundancies, flow-constitutions (American liquidity-order, Chinese
production-logistics-order, Russian physical-substrate-order), the deactivation of the polis-state
mediation layer, the relationship between Brzezinski's anticipated coalition and the present three-pole
configuration, and the scaling question that points beyond the terrestrial system. Section VI states the
analytical claim: that the territorial categories that organized two centuries of strategic thought no longer
constitute the load-bearing layer, and that a reading centered on flow captures dynamics the territorial
frame structurally cannot.

title: The Economic Impact of the Warner Bros. – Paramount Skydance Theater Commitment
affiliations: The Jack Kemp Foundation, Independent and University of Wisconsin - Whitewater - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Economic Impact of the Warner Bros. – Paramount Skydance Theater Commitment
detail.abstract:
Earlier this year, Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance announced they would enter into a merger, with one of the promises being a commitment to having more movies appear in theaters before being made available via streaming. Upon completion of the merger, the new company plans to introduce 30 theatrical releases each year—15 by each studio—with a 45-day window before the movies can be streamed. On June 12th the Justice Department provisionally approved the merger, but several state Attorneys General have yet to give their approval. 

Our analysis estimates that the annual production of 30 films by a combined Warner Bros. Discovery–Paramount Skydance entity that are distributed in a theater would generate nearly $12.3 billion in total economic activity, including about $2.7 billion in direct studio spending and roughly $9.5 billion in indirect and induced effects spread across the broader U.S. economy. This production activity would directly support over 7,000 jobs and an additional 39,000 jobs through indirect/included supply lines, while producing an estimated $1.9 billion in federal, state, and local tax revenue. 

We find that the commitment of a 45-day theatrical window would boost local cinema revenue while also bolstering upstream and downstream industries. The theatrical release of 30 films annually would generate over $7.3 billion in additional economic activity, including more than $2.6 billion in ticket sales and $4.75 billion in related spending across restaurants, suppliers, travel, and other industries. This activity would support roughly 25,000 theater jobs and create nearly 20,000 more jobs in ancillary sectors while generating nearly $1 billion in tax revenue per annum. 

The Wisconsin-specific effects around the longer distribution for these 30 films amount to over 800 jobs and $136 million in GDP spending spread across the State. 

As the movie theater industry is still returning to form from the COVID-19 shutdowns, the merger would reinforce the growing industry by providing a consistent stream of content while also boosting spending in connected sectors. On the whole, we estimate an annual stimulus of nearly $20 billion through the support of over 90,000 jobs spread across the U.S. Ultimately, the proposed plan would create an environment of predictability for theaters in what has been a volatile business.

title: Two Indias, One GDP: How Billionaire Wealth is Masking the Middle Class Crisis

detail.title: Two Indias, One GDP: How Billionaire Wealth is Masking the Middle Class Crisis
detail.abstract: In 2025, India celebrated becoming one of the world's largest economies by GDP. This paper argues that the celebration obscures more than it reveals. Drawing on data from the World Inequality Lab, IMF, Reserve Bank of India, Oxfam India, and the National Statistical Office, this paper examines the growing disconnect between India's aggregate economic growth and the lived reality of its 1.46 billion people. India's top 1 percent holds 40 percent of national wealth, while the bottom half shares just 3 percent. The paper documents the specific pressures facing India's middle class: stagnating wages, household debt at 41.3 percent of GDP, housing costs consuming over 40 percent of monthly income, and food inflation hitting lower-income households disproportionately. It argues that GDP is fundamentally inadequate for assessing whether economic growth improves ordinary lives, and proposes three concrete policy interventions: adoption of a Multidimensional Welfare Index alongside GDP, mandatory publication of quarterly median income data, and a compulsory inequality impact assessment for every major budget announcement.

title: Too Old to Train?Age Differences in Employer-Provided Training:Experimental Evidence from Italian SMEs
affiliations: Bocconi University, Bocconi University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Too Old to Train?Age Differences in Employer-Provided Training:Experimental Evidence from Italian SMEs
detail.abstract: Older workers are among the most expensive employees on firms’ payrolls — yetthey are systematically the least likely to receive employer-provided training. This paperinvestigates the managerial decisions that generate this paradox through two complementary surveys conducted among Italian small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Thefirst survey documents a strong, monotonic age gradient in training allocation: employees’probability of being selected for training decreases sharply with age. Motivated bythese findings, the second survey introduces a randomized information treatment: managersreceive information on labor-force aging, rising retirement ages, and the remainingworking life of older workers. This information does not reduce managers’ age gradientin training allocation, suggesting that this bias is sustained by mechanisms other thansimple horizon-based considerations.

title: The Triad of Tech Sovereignty and Europe's Package: Dependency, Openness, and Agency
affiliations: The GovLab and

detail.title: The Triad of Tech Sovereignty and Europe's Package: Dependency, Openness, and Agency

declarations.ethicsApproval: NA

detail.abstract:
On June 3, 2026, the European Commission presented its Technological Sovereignty Package (IP/26/1187), marking a pivotal shift in recognizing digital infrastructure not just as an economic asset but as a vital source of geopolitical power. This paper provides an early assessment of the Package through what we call the Triad of Tech Sovereignty. This framework highlights that the battle for technological sovereignty unfolds across three intertwined dimensions: dependency, openness and agency. 

Evaluating Europe's Package against this Triad reveals strong measures addressing dependency and a notable push towards openness. However, the dimension of agency is underdeveloped, or rather misallocated, with critical decision-making relegated to national administrations and insufficient mechanisms for participation, redress, or enforcement. 

We claim that viewing sovereignty purely through the lens of infrastructure ownership misses the core issue: the crucial factor is who has the power to shape, govern, and challenge these systems. Since the concentration of power is a choice, not an unavoidable outcome, merely creating new asymmetries won't solve the problem. Leveraging the principle of digital self-determination, we propose a "stewardship architecture": a nuanced framework of engagements and oversight mechanisms rooted in existing EU law. This approach would allow Europe to prioritize agency, rather than mere ownership, as the true measure of its digital sovereignty, empowering its citizens and institutions in the process.

detail.abstract: Recent debates surrounding artificial intelligence, consciousness, and alternative scientific models reveal a growing instability in the language used to describe machine intelligence, research originality, and the status of independent inquiry. This paper argues that the problem is not confined to independent researchers or popular media. It also appears in academic environments when researchers conflate intelligence, language production, computation, cognition, agency, and consciousness. The most serious expression of this confusion is the premature claim of “hybrid consciousness”, where human consciousness and artificial intelligence are treated as if they belong to a continuous category. The paper rejects this move as a category error and proposes a scientific distinction between AI as a system of computational and statistical-symbolic performance and consciousness as a biologically, affectively, and subjectively situated condition. It further develops a methodological distinction between AI as a legitimate research tool and AI as an intellectual crutch. The paper concludes that AI can assist organisation, comparison, formatting, searching, and structural analysis, but it cannot replace human judgement, evidential responsibility, conceptual clarity, falsifiability, or authorship accountability.

title: Next-Generation RegTech: AI-Driven Cybersecurity and Data Governance for Real-Time Compliance Intelligence Author

detail.title: Next-Generation RegTech: AI-Driven Cybersecurity and Data Governance for Real-Time Compliance Intelligence Author

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper explores the emerging paradigm of next-generation Regulatory Technology (RegTech), focusing on the integration of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity systems, and data governance frameworks to enable real-time compliance intelligence. As regulatory environments become increasingly complex and data-intensive, traditional compliance mechanisms are proving insufficient in addressing dynamic risks, cross-border data flows, and rapidly evolving cyber threats. The study examines how AI-driven systems can transform compliance from a reactive and periodic function into a continuous, automated, and predictive process. It further investigates the role of advanced cybersecurity architectures in safeguarding regulatory data integrity while ensuring adaptive compliance monitoring across digital ecosystems. In addition, the paper analyzes data governance models that support transparency, auditability, and regulatory accountability in AI-enabled environments. By synthesizing insights from information systems, cybersecurity management, and digital governance literature, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for real-time compliance intelligence. This framework highlights the convergence of machine learning algorithms, automated risk detection systems, and governance protocols to enhance regulatory responsiveness and operational resilience. The findings contribute to both academic discourse and industry practice by outlining how organizations can transition toward intelligent compliance infrastructures that reduce regulatory friction, improve risk visibility, and support proactive decision-making in highly regulated digital environments.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital ecosystems, cloud-native infrastructures, artificial intelligence (AI), and data-intensive business operations has significantly increased the complexity of regulatory compliance across industries. Traditional compliance approaches, which often rely on manual audits, periodic assessments, and fragmented governance processes, struggle to keep pace with evolving cyber threats, expanding regulatory frameworks, and the growing volume of organizational data. These challenges have accelerated the emergence of Regulatory Technology (RegTech) solutions designed to automate compliance processes and enhance organizational transparency. However, the next generation of RegTech extends beyond automation by integrating AI-driven cybersecurity capabilities and advanced data governance frameworks to create real-time compliance intelligence systems. This article explores the evolution of Next-Generation RegTech as a strategic convergence of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity risk management, and data governance. The study examines how machine learning algorithms, predictive analytics, security automation, continuous monitoring platforms, and governance-as-code architectures enable organizations to identify regulatory risks, detect compliance violations, and respond to emerging threats in real time. Furthermore, the article investigates the role of explainable AI, privacy-preserving technologies, automated control validation, and intelligent audit systems in strengthening regulatory oversight and organizational accountability. The research highlights how AI-enhanced cybersecurity mechanisms contribute to compliance resilience by continuously assessing vulnerabilities, monitoring anomalous activities, and mitigating cyber risks before they escalate into regulatory incidents. Simultaneously, robust data governance frameworks ensure data quality, integrity, lineage, privacy, and policy enforcement across increasingly distributed digital environments. Through the integration of these capabilities, organizations can transition from reactive compliance management to proactive and predictive compliance intelligence. The findings suggest that Next-Generation RegTech provides significant advantages in terms of operational efficiency, regulatory adaptability, risk visibility, and stakeholder trust. By enabling continuous compliance monitoring and intelligent decision support, AI-driven RegTech platforms position organizations to address future regulatory challenges while supporting secure and responsible digital innovation. The article concludes by proposing a framework for implementing real-time compliance intelligence as a foundational capability for modern digital enterprises.

detail.abstract: Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant challenges to modern legal systems due to the rapid growth of digital technologies and online transactions. India has witnessed a substantial increase in cyber offences including hacking, identity theft, phishing, ransomware attacks, cyber terrorism, online fraud, and privacy violations. This paper examines the legal framework governing cyber crimes in India with particular reference to the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and related evidentiary provisions. The study analyses important judicial pronouncements that have shaped cyber law jurisprudence and evaluates the challenges faced by investigation agencies in detecting, investigating, and prosecuting cyber offences. A comparative analysis of international approaches highlights gaps in the Indian enforcement mechanism, particularly regarding digital forensics, cross-border cooperation, and technological expertise. The paper further identifies major loopholes in the existing framework and proposes reforms such as specialized cyber police units, enhanced forensic infrastructure, capacity building, stronger data protection measures, and international cooperation mechanisms. The study concludes that effective cybercrime prevention requires a combination of robust legal provisions, technological advancement, institutional capacity, and public awareness to ensure a secure digital environment while safeguarding constitutional rights and freedoms.

title: "WhatsApp University": Digital Trust, Kinship Epistemology, and the Architecture of Misinformation in India

detail.title: "WhatsApp University": Digital Trust, Kinship Epistemology, and the Architecture of Misinformation in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies entirely on the synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, publicly available secondary data, and aggregated industry reports. No direct human participants or animals were involved, and therefore formal ethical approval was not required.
