detail.abstract: India represents the world's largest WhatsApp market, with an estimated 500-550 million monthly active users as of 2024, yet it simultaneously exhibits one of the most acute and well-documented crises of messaging-mediated misinformation on the planet. This paper introduces the Kinship Epistemology Model (KEM)-a formal framework that explains why Indian users systematically trust algorithmically unverified content forwarded by socially proximate senders over verified reports from institutional news sources. Drawing on secondary data from the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2024, the Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review, the Edelman Trust Barometer 2024, Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) subscriber data, and a structured synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, we demonstrate that trust in WhatsApp news is not a failure of individual rationality but a structurally coherent response to three compounding conditions: declining institutional media credibility, the social architecture of the joint-family and community group, and the affective economy of the forward-message gesture. We formalise the concept of the Trust-Transmission Amplification Factor (TTAF) and the Misinformation Persistence Index (MPI), propose a typological taxonomy of circulating content across four categories, and show through empirical synthesis that standard fact-checking interventions fail because they target epistemic errors while the underlying mechanism is affective validation. The paper concludes with a policy framework-the Source-Agnostic Emotional Correction (SAEC) protocol-designed to match the emotional architecture through which misinformation spreads. These contributions together constitute what we term the KEM-TTAF theoretical system, a potentially foundational framework for the emerging field of dark-social epistemology.

title: How Firms Communicate Artificial Intelligence in Earnings Calls: Opportunities, Risks, and Market Reactions
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong (CityU), National University of Singapore - Department of Information Systems and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: How Firms Communicate Artificial Intelligence in Earnings Calls: Opportunities, Risks, and Market Reactions
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a prominent focus of corporate disclosures in earnings conference calls, yet informational value of such disclosures remains difficult for external stakeholders to evaluate. Rather than examining whether firms mention AI, this study investigates how firms communicate AI opportunities and risks. We develop a human-in-theloop generative AI framework integrating domain-specific dictionaries with LLM-based annotation to systematically analyze AI-related disclosures. We find that AI opportunity disclosures are positively associated with cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), driven primarily by AI exploitation opportunities, while competitive and operational AI risk disclosures are negatively associated with CAR. Over longer horizons, AI opportunity disclosures predict superior firm performance, while the negative relationship between AI risk disclosures and firm performance attenuates. Disclosure specificity and unscripted AI disclosure further moderate these relationships. This study shifts attention from AI adoption to strategic external communication, contributing to the literature on AI business value, fintech, and corporate disclosure.

title: Persistent Threats, Fragile Defenses: An Analysis of Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities in Nigeria's Government and Banking Sectors (2024-2026)
affiliations: Ladoke Akintola University of Technology

detail.title: Persistent Threats, Fragile Defenses: An Analysis of Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities in Nigeria's Government and Banking Sectors (2024-2026)
detail.abstract: Nigeria's government agencies and banking institutions experienced an accelerating wave of cybersecurity breaches between 2024 and 2026, occurring against a backdrop of rapid digital transformation and expanding e-government infrastructure. This paper investigates why these breaches continue to recur despite the existence of relevant legislation, including the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and the Cybercrime Amendment Act 2024, and proposes a framework of structural interventions to reduce systemic vulnerability. Drawing on five case studies spanning the National Bureau of Statistics website defacement of December 2024, the ongoing monetization of NIMC identity data through licensed intermediaries, the Killsec ransomware attack on Princeps Credit Systems in September 2025, the ByteToBreach attack chain that traversed Sterling Bank, Remita, and the Corporate Affairs Commission between March and April 2026, and the broader dark web commodification of Nigerian institutional data across 2025, the paper identifies five interconnected root causes: elementary credential management failures in regulated financial infrastructure, inadequate governance of third-party and insider access, an institutional response culture that consistently prioritizes opacity over accountability, a structural cybersecurity talent shortage accelerated by professional emigration, and a regulatory enforcement model that remains reactive rather than proactive. The paper advances six targeted recommendations addressed to the Central Bank of Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, the National Information Technology Development Agency, and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy. These recommendations include the mandatory adoption of secure development standards, a national third-party access governance framework, reform of breach notification enforcement, Zero Trust Architecture as the baseline for government digital platforms, a national cybersecurity talent retention programme, and a public-private cyber threat intelligence sharing platform. Nigeria's experience in this period offers a case study of relevance beyond its borders, illustrating the systemic risks that emerge when digital infrastructure expansion outpaces the institutional capacity to secure it.

title: What Science Is, Information Systems Research Is Not

detail.title: What Science Is, Information Systems Research Is Not
detail.abstract: Information Systems calls itself a science. It publishes in journals, conducts peer review, applies methods, builds on prior work, and claims relevance to practice. But publication is not knowledge, peer review is not verification, method is not scrutiny, citation is not cumulativeness, and implications for practice are not consequence. I argue that IS has confused the products of research with the practices of science, building an extensive publication system without building a checking system that would make its outputs scientific. Drawing on the philosophy of science, I show that IS research fails the conditions its own claims require: that findings can be checked, corrected, built upon, and used by the people they claim to inform. The result is an epistemic crisis: a largely unverified literature whose reliability we cannot assess because we never built the means to check it. Viva la IS Revolution.

title: From Informal Work Routines to Strategic HR Architecture: An SOP-Based, KPI-Driven HR Blueprint for Sustainable Competitive Advantage in a Coffee Shop SME
affiliations: Universitas Sulawesi Barat, Universitas Sulawesi Barat and Universitas Sulawesi Barat

detail.title: From Informal Work Routines to Strategic HR Architecture: An SOP-Based, KPI-Driven HR Blueprint for Sustainable Competitive Advantage in a Coffee Shop SME
detail.abstract: This paper develops an integrated strategic human resource blueprint for a coffee shop small and mediumsized enterprise (SME) by examining how informal people-management routines constrain service consistency, employee accountability, and sustainable competitiveness. The study responds to a persistent gap in strategic human resource management (SHRM) research: while SHRM scholarship has established the value of internally aligned HR systems, less is known about how resource-constrained food and beverage SMEs can translate strategic HR principles into simple, low-cost, and operationally usable governance mechanisms. Using a qualitative single-case study of Maio Coffee & Eatery in Majene, West Sulawesi, the research draws on interviews, HR practice audit, SWOT analysis, strategic fit analysis, and gap analysis. The findings reveal a clear strategic misfit between the firm's service-quality ambition and its informal HR practices. Recruitment is network-based, training is experiential, performance evaluation is subjective, compensation is fixed, and employee communication lacks governance. The most critical gaps are the absence of documented Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and measurable Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The proposed HR Blueprint integrates SOP-based HR governance, a KPI-driven performance system, employee development and engagement routines, and simple digital HR analytics using Google Forms and spreadsheets. Practically, the model enables SME owners to standardize service behavior, diagnose performance gaps, reduce dependence on individual employees, and build a scalable human-capital infrastructure. The paper contributes by theorizing a low-cost HR architecture for coffee shop SMEs that connects SHRM, strategic fit, human capital development, and service competitiveness.

title: Recursive Cultivation Theory

detail.title: Recursive Cultivation Theory
detail.abstract: Classical cultivation theory explained how prolonged exposure to patterned television worlds could shape viewers' perceptions of social reality. In AI-mediated environments, exposure alone no longer describes the object of analysis. Algorithmic feeds, recommender systems, conversational agents, generative content pipelines, moderation layers, and personalization systems adapt to user behavior and then return modified environments to the user. This manuscript proposes Recursive Cultivation Theory, a cultivation-theory overhaul for adaptive media systems. The central claim is that modern media systems cultivate humans while humans cultivate the systems that later cultivate them. The appropriate unit of analysis is not isolated content, but the longitudinal calibration trajectory of the human-medium loop. The paper distinguishes influence, cultivation, effective structural commitment, outcome architecture, and decision custody: local shifts in attention or belief; repeated shaping of priors, salience, habits, affect, and expressive norms; accumulated narrowing of practically available futures even when formal choice remains; deliberate design of conditions that repeatedly produce beneficial outcomes; and enforceable control over the transition from recommendation or record to consequential action. It introduces public-cognitive health as a domain concerned with population-level reality contact, belief reversibility, attention integrity, cultural legibility, neurocognitive plurality, repair capacity, and value creation. The framework treats guardrails as cultivation operators, not merely safety filters, and integrates the double empathy problem, central-coherence diversity, monotropism, recursive masking pressure, neurotype-preserving calibration, incentive alignment, ownership, systemic orchestration, and receipt-based governance. It argues that the deepest risk of AI-mediated media is not only false content, but recursive miscalibration: loops that make correction harder, optionality thinner, custody less inspectable, and machine legibility look like human validity. It further argues that mature governance cannot stop at policy language or failure prevention. It must reach the control surface: who had authority, what was allowed or refused, what evidence was used, what consequence was committed or withheld, and whether an independent reviewer can reconstruct the transition from the receipt alone. The manuscript concludes with a research agenda and governance controls for measuring calibration drift, structural narrowing, feedback-signal ambiguity, synthetic-data contamination, guardrail distortion, incentive misalignment, ownership gaps, systemic orchestration failure, custody gaps, receipt insufficiency, and intervention capacity before trajectories harden.

title:
The Auditor's Dilemma: 
Strategic Ambiguity, Legibility, and the Deterrence-liability Tension under a Single Reputation Working Paper

detail.title:
The Auditor's Dilemma: 
Strategic Ambiguity, Legibility, and the Deterrence-liability Tension under a Single Reputation Working Paper
detail.abstract: A single auditor manages one reputation before two audiences who read the same detection capability through different functionals: deterrence requires that management believe detection is high, while liability limitation requires that a court be unable to prove it was. Decomposing capability into actual, perceived, and verifiable levels, we show that strategic ambiguity is the unique instrument that opens a wedge between belief (a mean) and enforcement (a worst case). Because investors both reward the reputation and litigate its betrayal, the reputational level is double-edged and self-limiting; only the spread separates the two demands. Capability is privately under-supplied through hidden action; documentation, the standard-setter's indirect lever, yields genuine improvement only when records are informative, and the long-run failure rate is pinned by the regulatory ratchet, not by capability. Artificial intelligence raises capability while withdrawing legibility, resetting the tension one level higher: the expectation gap migrates from auditor to model.

title: Strategic Management and Organizational Performance: A Systematic Review of the Scientific Literature
affiliations: Universidad Nacional de Frontera, Universidad Cesar Vallejo (UCV), Universidad Nacional de Frontera and Universidad Nacional de Frontera

detail.title: Strategic Management and Organizational Performance: A Systematic Review of the Scientific Literature
detail.abstract: Strategic management has established itself as a fundamental element for strengthening organizational performance in an environment characterized by globalization, digital transformation and growing business competitiveness. In this context, the objective of this research was to analyze and synthesize the available scientific evidence on the relationship between strategic management and organizational performance through a systematic review of the literature. The methodology was developed under the guidelines of the PRISMA 2020 declaration, using Google Scholar as the main source of information. The initial search identified 200 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025, of which, after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 20 studies were selected for the final analysis. The results showed that strategic management positively influences organizational performance by favoring competitiveness, efficiency, innovation, and business sustainability. Likewise, it was identified that strategic planning, strategic leadership, organizational culture, and dynamic capabilities are the most relevant factors associated with organizational success. The bibliometric analysis revealed that the main research topics focus on strategic management, organizational performance, competitiveness, sustainability and digital transformation. It is concluded that strategic management represents an integral process that allows organizations to adapt to changing environments, strengthen their competitive advantages and improve their institutional results, constituting a key factor for sustainability and long-term organizational growth.

title:
Stoic Leadership Under Legal Uncertainty 
Inner Self-Regulation as the Foundation of Executive Responsibility

detail.title:
Stoic Leadership Under Legal Uncertainty 
Inner Self-Regulation as the Foundation of Executive Responsibility
detail.abstract: Executive leadership increasingly takes place under conditions of legal ambiguity. Formal norms are supplemented or partially replaced by soft law, political expectations, and de-facto binding effects. The structure of responsibility shifts: external clarity declines while the individual decision burden on the actors rises. This article develops a Stoic-psychological model of leadership that reconstructs executive decision-making as a function of inner self-regulation. Drawing on the Stoic Self Regulation Framework (SSRF), it models leadership as a multi-level process linking external conditions, perceived control, inner judgment, and concrete action. Under legal uncertainty, responsibility shifts from the level of norms to the level of personality. Executive integrity does not arise from expanding formal power but from the coherence of inner judgment, emotional stability, and value-oriented conduct.

title: Strategic HR Blueprint for Competitive Advantage in SME Food and Beverage: An HR Audit and Strategic Human Resource Planning in a Family-Owned Café
affiliations: Universitas Sulawesi Barat, Universitas Sulawesi Barat and Universitas Sulawesi Barat

detail.title: Strategic HR Blueprint for Competitive Advantage in SME Food and Beverage: An HR Audit and Strategic Human Resource Planning in a Family-Owned Café
detail.abstract: Background: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the food and beverage sector, particularly coffee shops and dining establishments, frequently operate with informal and unstructured human resource (HR) management practices that constrain their service quality, employee productivity, and long-term competitive positioning. Purpose: This study investigates the current state of HR practices at Cafe Diaz, a family-owned café in Majene, West Sulawesi, Indonesia, and proposes a comprehensive Strategic HR Blueprint to bridge identified gaps and enhance organizational competitiveness. Method: A qualitative case study approach was employed, incorporating structured in-depth interviews with the owner-manager, direct field observation, HR audit procedures, SWOT analysis, strategic fit analysis, and gap analysis. Data were triangulated to ensure trustworthiness. Findings: The audit revealed a complete absence of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), competency-based recruitment, structured training, and transparent compensation systems. A comprehensive misalignment was identified between the business strategy and all HR practice dimensions. The proposed HR Blueprint integrates four novelty components: (1) SOP-based HR Governance, (2) KPI-Driven Performance Management, (3) Simple Digital HR Analytics utilizing zero-cost platforms, and (4) an Integrated HR Blueprint Model specifically designed for coffee shop businesses. Practical Implications: The blueprint offers a scalable, low-resourceintensive transformation pathway applicable to family-owned F&B SMEs in developing economies. Originality/Value: This study contributes an empirically grounded, context-sensitive HR transformation framework for informally-managed SMEs in Indonesia's emerging service economy, addressing a significant gap in SHRM literature focusing on micro-enterprise contexts in non-metropolitan settings.

title: The ⿻  Plural Stack: Rebuilding Our Digital Foundations from Protocol Up
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Global Solutions Initiative Foundation GmbH and RadicalxChange Foundation

detail.title: The ⿻  Plural Stack: Rebuilding Our Digital Foundations from Protocol Up
detail.abstract: Europe stands at a critical juncture in the digital age. US Big Tech and Chinese state capitalism dominate global digital infrastructure, whilst the bloc is challenged by systemic vulnerabilities, extractive economics, and strategic dependencies. However, blaming 'foreign' digital infrastructure misidentifies the challenge; it's not about the foreign origin of digital platforms but the architectural logic of technical centralisation, economic extraction, and the funneling of decision making power. Our vision of a European digital stack demands a strategic imperative towards Plural protocol ecosystems, offering a properties-driven framework to design, identify and build plural protocols across three independent but intertwined dimensions: the technical, economic and social. The aim is to build open and decentralised technologies, fair and non-extractive economic models, and plural, participatory communities-for every layer of the stack. Using our established framework, Plurality addresses each structural problem. Systemic vulnerability becomes infrastructural resilience, economic extraction becomes competitiveness, and strategic dependency becomes shared sovereignty. Beyond Europe, democratic middle powers and like-minded allies equally possess the capacity to collaboratively forge a distinct third path – one that embeds human rights, digital rights, sustainability, democratic subsidiarity, and proportionality into shared infrastructure. Drawing on successful models, including Taiwan's digital democracy and emerging initiatives in the decentralised open source space, we propose a framework that operationalises democratic values through technology in a globally enforceable way. This broad conception of platform power demands a policy response that goes beyond competition law alone. This paper proposes concrete policy recommendations for building self-sustaining Plural protocol ecosystems; covering public infrastructure investment, fiscal instruments, interoperability mandates, legal forms for decentralised organisations, and procurement targets, proposing a strategy of transformation by existing platform actors, rather than exclusion.

title: The Gravity of Convergence: How Counter Theses Find Each Other Without Surrendering Themselves

detail.title: The Gravity of Convergence: How Counter Theses Find Each Other Without Surrendering Themselves
detail.abstract: This paper proposes and examines a phenomenon termed dialectical convergence under pressure: the process by which opposing ideological or strategic theses do not defeat each other but are mutually transformed through sustained encounter, producing entities that carry the structural DNA of both originals while being reducible to neither. Distinct from Hegelian synthesis-which implies a clean third formation-and from institutional isomorphism-which describes surface-level mimicry under legitimacy pressure-dialectical convergence denotes a deeper, often generative co-mutation of opposing systems. The paper develops a three-part theoretical framework and illustrates its application across three domains: (i) the political economy of China's socialist market transition, where Dengist pragmatism dissolved the capitalism-socialism binary through strategic ambiguity rather than resolution; (ii) the convergence of India's two dominant political formations-Congress and the BJP-on welfare statism and civilizational nationalism despite nominally opposite founding ideologies; and (iii) three business case studies-Microsoft's absorption of open source, Netflix's reconvergence with linear television, and Amazon's strategic re-entry into physical retail-where counter-model competitors transformed each other through competitive proximity. The paper argues that convergence quality is determined by whether the original tension survives within the new formation: where it does, convergence is generative and adaptive; where one thesis absorbs the other without mutual transformation, the result is colonisation dressed as synthesis. The paper concludes with a proposed typology of convergence modes and implications for strategic theory and political economy.

title: Evolving Fraud Networks in North American Businesses

detail.title: Evolving Fraud Networks in North American Businesses
detail.abstract:
This intelligence brief examines the evolution of cyber fraud networks operating within North American digital ecosystems, with particular emphasis on Business Email Compromise (BEC), AI-generated employment scams, and cryptocurrency-enabled laundering. The report analyzes how fraud actors have transitioned from traditional social-engineering schemes into scalable, technology-driven operations targeting businesses, immigrants, and international students across Canada and the United States. 

Key trends identified include the increasing use of synthetic recruiter identities, fake LinkedIn job postings, deepfake-assisted impersonation, and payment-diversion tactics linked to mule accounts and digital asset laundering pathways. The study further explores how rapid digital hiring practices, remote onboarding systems, and decentralized cryptocurrency infrastructure have expanded operational opportunities for transnational fraud actors. 

Findings suggest that existing Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and fraud-detection systems remain insufficiently equipped to identify relationship-based recruitment fraud and AI-assisted impersonation techniques. The report concludes that enhanced cross-border intelligence sharing, behavioral analytics integration, cryptocurrency forensic capabilities, and targeted public awareness initiatives are necessary to mitigate the growing operational sophistication of modern cyber-enabled financial crime networks.

title: Financial Strategy and Market Analysis in a Small Finance Firm: A Study of Gaps in Investment Decision-Making

detail.title: Financial Strategy and Market Analysis in a Small Finance Firm: A Study of Gaps in Investment Decision-Making
detail.abstract: This paper looks at the financial strategy and market analysis practices of a small Mumbaibased finance firm employing roughly ten to fifteen people across insurance and equity advisory work, referred to here as "the Firm." Despite steady profitability, four practical habits limit how well the Firm can compete for newer, faster-growing business: client and portfolio data are tracked in separate spreadsheets rather than one shared model; investment choices lean on what has historically performed well rather than where markets are heading; risk is described in words such as "high" or "low" rather than measured in numbers; and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) considerations rarely factor into how new investments are screened. Drawing on a two-month internship inside the Firm's planning team, informal conversations with colleagues, and published industry research on spreadsheet risk, ESG performance, and competitive pressure from fintech-driven advisors, this paper traces how these four habits show up day to day and what they likely cost the Firm in missed opportunity and unmeasured risk. It closes with four changes the Firm could realistically make without a large technology budget: a shared financial model in place of personal spreadsheets, a simple way to bring forward-looking market data into capital decisions, a basic numeric risk-scoring step, and a short ESG checklist for new investments.

title: Adaptive digital nudging improves caregiver engagement at scale: experimental evidence from India

detail.title: Adaptive digital nudging improves caregiver engagement at scale: experimental evidence from India

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Stern School of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: New York University Stern School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Public programs increasingly use digital messaging to sustain household engagement, but it remains unclear whether adaptive personalization adds value over simpler randomized outreach when interventions must operate through existing service-delivery infrastructure. In early childhood education, India's Anganwadi system comprises approximately 1.4 million community centers serving more than 100 million registered beneficiaries, so small engagement gains can translate into large absolute increases in program reach. We evaluate whether a deployed adaptive individualized messaging policy improves caregiver engagement beyond a nonadaptive randomized one-to-one messaging benchmark. In partnership with Rocket Learning, a nonprofit supporting early childhood learning through WhatsApp groups linked to Anganwadi centers across 16 Indian states, we conduct a preregistered field experiment across 24,778 WhatsApp groups comprising 156,429 caregivers. Groups are randomized to no experimental nudging, nonadaptive randomized one-to-one nudging, or adaptive one-to-one nudging. Both active policies used the same platform and message library, but the nonadaptive policy assigned a common random nudge within each active group-week whereas the adaptive policy individualized messages over time using observed engagement. The adaptive policy increases weekly active caregivers by 6.11% relative to control and outperforms the nonadaptive randomized benchmark by 3.70% on the primary outcome. Gains are concentrated among caregivers with prior but inconsistent engagement and in districts combining high digital access with weaker village-level service infrastructure. These results show that adaptive digital outreach can improve behavioral engagement at population scale, with additional adaptive premium in settings where households are reachable but generic randomized messaging leaves engagement gaps.

title: Digital Pathology as an Organizational Paradox: Digital Transformation, Professional Work, and Governance in Healthcare
affiliations: Stuttgart Clinic and University of Bern

detail.title: Digital Pathology as an Organizational Paradox: Digital Transformation, Professional Work, and Governance in Healthcare
detail.abstract: Digital pathology is commonly described as a technological transition from glass slides to whole-slide images. However, this framing underestimates the organizational complexity of transforming diagnostic pathology into a digitally mediated practice. Digital pathology changes not only the diagnostic medium but also the organization of work, the distribution of responsibility, the relationship between standardization and professional judgment, the dependence on technical infrastructure, and the future conditions for artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostics. This conceptual review proposes that digital pathology is best understood as an organizational paradox: a transformation process in which contradictory but interdependent demands coexist and persist over time. Drawing on paradox theory, particularly the dynamic equilibrium model of Smith and Lewis, the article identifies six core tensions in digital pathology: efficiency versus infrastructure dependency, standardization versus professional autonomy, automation versus expertise, innovation versus diagnostic confidence, flexibility versus organizational embeddedness, and workforce relief versus work intensification. These tensions should not be interpreted as implementation failures. They are structural features of digital transformation in a safety-critical diagnostic environment. Successful implementation therefore depends not on eliminating paradoxes but on managing them productively through resilient infrastructure, workflow automation, preserved diagnostic agency, quality governance, participatory change management, responsible integration of artificial intelligence, and mindset change. This framework contributes to technology-and-society scholarship by showing how digital transformation in a safety-critical professional domain produces persistent tensions between efficiency, dependency, autonomy, automation, innovation, and trust. Digital pathology is used as a theoretically informative case for understanding how organizations can govern digital technologies without reducing professional responsibility or system reliability.

title: Liberalising Discrimination Law
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Liberalising Discrimination Law
detail.abstract: Liberalising Discrimination Law examines the evolution and consequences of anti-discrimination legislation in the United Kingdom, arguing that the current legal framework has expanded beyond its original purpose of preventing unfair treatment. The authors contend that contemporary discrimination law increasingly regulates private decision-making and contractual freedom, creating legal uncertainty, compliance costs, and restrictions on individual and organisational autonomy. Drawing on legal analysis, policy discussion, and case examples, the paper argues for a narrower, more liberal conception of discrimination law that focuses on protecting core civil rights while reducing state intervention in voluntary associations, employment practices, and commercial relationships. The authors propose reforms intended to simplify the legal framework, strengthen freedom of association and expression, and restore greater scope for private choice. The work situates these arguments within a broader classical liberal critique of regulatory expansion and raises questions about how liberal democracies should balance equality objectives with individual liberty and institutional autonomy.

detail.title: Board Diversity and Nonprofit Fundraising

detail.abstract: We explore the relationship between the gender and racial diversity of nonprofits and their fundraising in the United States between 2010 and 2024 using IRS 990/990-EZ filings. We focus on two measures of board diversity-gender diversity relative to a 50-50 standard and an entropy-based measure of racial and ethnic diversity-and a measure of the similarity between the board's racial and ethnic makeup and that of the local area in which the nonprofit is registered. We describe how these measures have changed over the period of our study and how they vary by organizational size. We then estimate the relationship between fundraising and these diversity measures using nonprofit and state-year fixed effects to examine the correlation between changes in diversity and changes in fundraising. We find strong correlations between the two measures of diversity and nonprofit fundraising. We conclude with an exploration of the degree to which this association might be driven by omitted variables or reverse causality.

detail.abstract: Several recent papers have claimed, backed by evidence gathered from the empirical analysis, that the surge in rural female employment in India post 2017 is largely or predominantly attributable to economic distress faced by rural households, reiterating such views expressed in a Report and some articles published earlier. This hypothesis of an economic-distress-driven surge in female employment in India's rural areas post-2017 is scrutinised in the present paper. Some arguments are made, findings of a few earlier studies are reported, and some data are presented that cast doubts on the validity of the aforesaid hypothesis.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven decisionsupport marketplace designed to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of cross-border product sourcing and supply chain management. As global markets become more competitive and supply networks more complex, timely and accurate decisions about supplier selection, pricing, and logistics have become critical to business success. The study reviews how AI and Machine Learning (ML) techniques-including linear regression, random forest, neural networks, K-Nearest Neighbours, K-Means clustering, and reinforcement learning-can support demand forecasting, supplier performance evaluation, price prediction, and risk management. Drawing on the literature and well-known industry examples such as Amazon and Walmart, the paper discusses the potential benefits of AI in cross-border sourcing, including faster decision-making, cost reduction, and improved supply chain resilience. It also examines key limitations, namely data quality and availability, the cost of technology adoption for small and medium enterprises, and data security and privacy risks. The paper concludes that AI can substantially strengthen crossborder supply chains, provided that data quality, affordability, and human-AI collaboration are adequately addressed.

title: From Data to Decisions in Surgery Scheduling: Machine Learning and Simulation for Sequencing Arthroplasty Patients
affiliations: Aalborg University - Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University, Aalborg University, Aalborg University Hospital and Aalborg University

detail.title: From Data to Decisions in Surgery Scheduling: Machine Learning and Simulation for Sequencing Arthroplasty Patients
detail.abstract:
Purpose: Efficient operating room (OR) scheduling depends on accurate prediction of duration of surgery (DOS) and effective sequencing strategies. In high-volume arthroplasty procedures, reliance on averages or surgeons’ DOS estimates can cause inefficiencies in resource allocation. This study develops an integrated framework combining machine learning (ML) DOS prediction with discrete-event simulation (DES) to support evidence-based sequencing and scheduling decisions.

Design/methodology/approach: A dataset of 3,233 hip and knee arthroplasty cases was analyzed using preoperative clinical, operational, and temporal features. Multiple ML models were tested for DOS prediction; performance and feature importance were evaluated using accuracy metrics, SHAP values, and partial dependence. Predicted DOS values were then applied within DES to compare sequencing strategies and assess impacts on completion times, and overtime in marginal conditions.

Findings: Extreme Gradient Boosting achieved the best predictive accuracy (Mean Absolute Error = 12.86, Root Mean Squared Error = 16.67, Buffer Accuracy = 68.73). Surgeon, procedure type, and temporal variables were key predictors. Simulation experiments revealed that no single sequencing strategy consistently minimized finish times; effectiveness depended on patient-specific and contextual factors. Marginal condition analysis identified opportunities for improved OR utilization and reduced overtime through tailored sequencing policies.

Originality/value: This study uniquely integrates ML-based DOS prediction with simulation-driven sequencing evaluation in arthroplasty surgery. The framework advances beyond subjective or average-based planning by enabling data-driven, case-specific scheduling. The approach is adaptable to other surgical specialties and can incorporate additional predictors or real-time data, offering a novel pathway toward intelligent scheduling systems that balance clinical priorities with operational efficiency.

title: Hybrid inventory management under deeply-uncertain demand using stochastic programming
affiliations: University of Sheffield, University of Alberta, University of Sheffield, University of Alberta and University of Sheffield - Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering

detail.title: Hybrid inventory management under deeply-uncertain demand using stochastic programming
detail.abstract: Poor inventory management and deeply uncertain demand continue to challenge vaccine and healthcare supply chains, yet periodic review and continuous monitoring are still largely studied separately. This study develops a hybrid ordering framework for vaccine inventory management that combines periodic review with out-of-cycle emergency replenishment in a stochastic programming model. Demand uncertainty is represented through forecast-generated demand trajectories, and the stochastic formulation determines unified policy parameters for regular and emergency orders under an objective that combines expected and worst-case costs. Computational results show that, relative to a perfect-information benchmark, the stochastic policy relies more on regular orders, maintains more stable service levels, and yields lower backlog across uncertain demand realisations, albeit at higher overall cost. Sensitivity analyses further show that review frequency and cost parameters shape both system performance and the coupling between regular and emergency ordering in settings with volatile demand and strict service-level requirements.

detail.title: Decentralized Justice in Football: An Operational Framework for Integrating Kleros Mechanism and Artificial Intelligence with Virtual Assistant Referee (VAR) Protocol
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines the integration of blockchain-based decentralized arbitration and
Artificial Intelligence (AI) into football officiating, proposing an operational framework to
complement the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) system for on-field decision-making and explores
off-field applications for institutional governance.

Design/methodology/approach – The research employs comparative case study analysis of
officiating outcomes in pre and post-VAR eras, identifying recurring patterns of interpretative drift
and technological limitations. Two experiments evaluate decision-making under Kleros incentive
structures, i.e., one involving human jurors operating within Schelling Coin mechanism, and
another deploying multiple AI agents to assess identical factual evidence. These findings
contribute to the development of normative frameworks for both on-field and off-field integration.

Findings – Kleros human jurors achieve consensus on subjective VAR incidents, while AI agents
align on facts but diverge on interpretation. VAR exhibits persistent interpretative drift and
precision paradoxes post-implementation. Proposed framework (i.e., solely juror-based
adjudication and hybrid AI-juror model) is viable for on-field hybrid integration and off-field
governance.

Originality/value – This article advances a comprehensive operational framework integrating
blockchain technology and AI with VAR and proposing specific pilot implementations in
competitions with infrastructural disparities.

title: Society-in-the-Loop: Participatory AI Regulation and Public Trust, Evidence from a Survey Experiment on AI in Healthcare in the UK

detail.abstract: Public trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is widely considered essential for its widespread societal acceptance and adoption, particularly in high-stakes public sector contexts such as healthcare. Yet, despite growing concerns about the technocratic nature of AI governance, the role of civil society participation in shaping trust in AI regulation remains understudied. This article examines how different forms of civil society participation in AI regulation affect public trust in both the regulatory process and the AI systems governed by it. It develops a multidimensional conceptual framework distinguishing participatory mechanisms by actor type, participation intensity, and stage of regulatory involvement, and tests it in a survey experiment with a representative UK sample using a scenario of AI-based patient prioritisation in public healthcare. The results provide causal evidence that civil society participation can enhance public trust in AI and its regulation, but these effects depend strongly on participation design. Participation by civil society organisations, particularly in active ex-post roles, such as auditing or formal complaint procedures, generates the largest trust-enhancing effects. By contrast, more limited forms of participation fail to increase trust and can even undermine it. The analysis highlights the importance of more inclusive and societally embedded approaches to AI governance for building public trust and offers scholars and policymakers across sectors an analytical tool for systematically comparing participatory mechanisms in regulatory design.

title: The Evolution of LGBTQ Rights in Constitutional Law: A Comparative Analysis of Equality, Dignity, and Fundamental Rights
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Evolution of LGBTQ Rights in Constitutional Law: A Comparative Analysis of Equality, Dignity, and Fundamental Rights
detail.abstract: The constitutional recognition of LGBTQ+ rights represents a significant milestone in modern legal and constitutional development. For much of history, legal and constitutional frameworks around the world either ignored the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals or subjected them to discrimination based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. Over time, changing societal perspectives, the growth of international human rights norms, and increasingly progressive judicial interpretations have played a crucial role in reshaping constitutional protections for these communities. This study explores the development of LGBTQ+ rights within constitutional law by conducting a comparative examination of key jurisdictions, including India, the United States, South Africa, Canada, and the broader European human rights system.

title: The Decision-Execution Layer Model (DLM): A Framework for Understanding Governance Failure

detail.title: The Decision-Execution Layer Model (DLM): A Framework for Understanding Governance Failure
detail.abstract: Governance systems frequently fail despite the existence of policies, regulations, monitoring mechanisms, and oversight structures. Conventional governance frameworks focus principally on risk identification, compliance, and control design. They explain how institutions detect risks, but provide limited insight into what happens after a risk becomes known. This paper introduces the Decision-Execution Layer Model (DLM), a governance architecture framework developed to explain how governance systems fail between the detection of a problem and the execution of a protective intervention. The DLM proposes that governance operates through seven interconnected layers-Mandate and Authority, Institutional Architecture, Signal Processing, Monitoring, Escalation, Decision, and Audit and Accountability-and that failures within or between these layers produce nine recurring governance failure patterns including Decision Orphans, Governance Drift, Escalation Blockage, and Intervention Gaps. The framework is positioned in relation to six established theoretical traditions: organisational accident theory (Reason, 1990, 1997), normalisation of deviance (Vaughan, 1996), normal accident theory (Perrow, 1984), high reliability organisation theory (Weick and Sutcliffe, 2007), implementation gap theory (Pressman and Wildavsky, 1973), and principal-agent theory (Jensen and Meckling, 1976). Preliminary empirical evidence from thirty cross-sector cases-spanning artificial intelligence, aviation, cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, and public administration-suggests that the DLM's failure categories apply with consistent analytical utility across domains, and that intervention failure is the dominant governance outcome, while escalation failure is the most common pathway through which intervention capability is lost. The paper argues that governance systems fail not because they cannot detect problems, but because they lack the execution architecture to convert signals into accountable action-a diagnosis that carries implications for governance design across sectors, institutions, and national contexts.

detail.abstract: Canada's Charitable Donations Tax Credit (CDTC), a $2+ billion annual tax expenditure, conditions access on CRA registration via common law public benefit tests administered through CG-011. This paper argues the CDTC is structurally biased against farmed animal welfare organizations, as eligibility relies on NFACC Codes of Practice (drafted by a board where animal agriculture holds 20/27 voting seats) and human-centered public benefit readings. Evaluating against Neil Brooks' four criteria (equity, neutrality, simplicity, accountability), informed by Pemsel fourth-head jurisprudence and the Senate's Catalyst for Change (2019), the CDTC fails each. It subsidizes status-quo charities while excluding challengers informed by public sentiment. detail.abstract: On a price-time-priority futures book a market maker earns a spread for supplying liquidity and pays adverse selection to the informed traders who pick off its quotes (Glosten-Milgrom). The empirical literature lacks a direct, large-scale, trueaggressor-signed measurement of how large that cost is relative to the captured spread. We supply one on CME depth-10 data (13 roots, 234 contract-days, 353,387 maker fills): a ground-truth, fill-by-fill maker-P&L decomposition splitting each passive fill into the half-spread captured at the touch (+0.654 bp) and the post-fill adverse drift the counterparty takes back (-0.661 bp). Adverse selection consumes essentially the whole captured half-spread, leaving net maker P&L indistinguishable from zero (-0.022 bp after the 0.015 bp fee, every root within ±0.13 bp). Because passive fills are charged no slippage and every unmodelled friction pushes net more negative, this is a one-sided bound: net ≤≈ 0 (Proposition 1). Read through a minimal competitive model the cancellation is consistent with the zero-profit condition of liquidity supply, and it carries a derived sufficient tick-size survival condition. The one-tick floor clears the fee only for the coarse-tick roots ZN and SI, beyond which the per-root adverse drift decides (the ≈ 0.74 bp frontier separating the survivors is descriptive, not a structural necessity). The sample concentrates in one calm 2023 month (93% of fills), so the cancellation is established cross-sectionally, within a single volatility regime. Whether the cancellation holds across volatility regimes is confounded by the resolution of the book reconstruction, which we resolve by measuring on a single nanosecond-resolution, true-aggressor-signed trades-and-quotes (TAQ) feed that spans the regimes we test and reproduces the depth-feed decomposition to 0.3pp on matched calm sessions. On that feed adverse selection over-consumes the captured spread in three crisis weeks (adverse-to-captured 105.1% SVB, 111.5% FOMC, 109.8% COVID, CIs excluding 100%) and net maker P&L deepens with volatility.

title: Killing the Case for Randomization in Dynamic Assortment Optimization
affiliations: and Cornell University - School of Operations Research and Information Engineering

detail.title: Killing the Case for Randomization in Dynamic Assortment Optimization
detail.abstract: One of the traditional approaches for constructing approximate policies for dynamic assortment optimization problems is to use sampling-based inventory-agnostic policies. Such policies are called sampling-based, as they sample an assortment of products from a fixed distribution at each time period to offer to a customer of each type. Such policies are called inventory-agnostic, as the sampled assortments may include products without remaining inventories, so if a customer chooses a product without remaining inventories, then she leaves without a purchase. Inventory-agnostic nature of a policy is not a concern, because it is known that if the policy samples an assortment that includes products without remaining inventories, then dropping the products without remaining inventories does not degrade the performance. However, sampling-based nature of a policy is a concern, because sampling brings another source of uncertainty in the performance and may erode trust in the platform. In this paper, we give an algorithm to de-randomize any sampling-based inventory-agnostic policy, so the de-randomized policy offers a deterministic sequence of assortments within the support of the original policy without degrading the performance. Furthermore, we give a variation of our de-randomization algorithm that searches for a deterministic sequence of assortments beyond the support of the original policy. We show that we can implement the latter variation efficiently as long as we can solve the static assortment optimization problem under the choice model governing the choice process of the customers. Either way, if the original policy has a performance guarantee, then the de-randomized policy performs at least just as well. As our crowning technical contribution, we study locally-optimal deterministic policies, where changing any single one of the assortments in the policy does not improve the total expected revenue. We show that any locally-optimal policy has a performance guarantee of 1/2-ϵ when compared with the best sampling-based policy. Noting that the best sampling-based policy has a constant factor performance guarantee, our result yields a fully novel approach for dynamic assortment optimization. Our computational work indicates that a de-randomized policy can substantially improve the original policy and working with assortments beyond the support of the original policy can be quite useful.

detail.abstract: We develop a continuous-time model of segmented bond markets to analyze the dual role of fixed-income exchange-traded funds (ETFs). ETFs provide liquidity hedging, compress OTC spreads, and enhance price discovery, particularly when underlying markets are impaired. Yet when authorized participants’ arbitrage capacity weakens, the model generates persistent price dislocations, path-dependent equilibria, and redemption-driven markdowns. This fragility operates through prices and arbitrage breakdown, not investor flows. The model rationalizes the concentration of March 2020 ETF-NAV discounts in safer, more liquid underlying markets. These vulnerabilities grow as ETFs expand across increasingly illiquid and opaque credit markets, with implications for financial stability.

title: Fitness, Cost, and Return: A Multi-Construct Framework for AI Governance

detail.title: Fitness, Cost, and Return: A Multi-Construct Framework for AI Governance
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Return on AI Investment (ROAI) ratio as a governance construct for AI deployment at organisational scale. The ROAI ratio is defined as the ratio of external fitness improvement attributable to AI deployment to total AI deployment cost — comprising compute cost and governance cost. It integrates three prior measurement constructs — the Q:F ratio (internal output quality relative to external organisational fitness), the IT:HR ratio (compute cost relative to governance cost), and Human Alignment Value (the contribution of human workers to AI alignment) — into a single return measure that addresses the question those constructs do not individually answer: whether AI deployment generates fitness improvement commensurate with its cost. The empirical motivation is drawn from documented cases of AI budget failure. Uber exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after an internal leaderboard incentivised token consumption rather than fitness improvement. Dell Technologies reported that token consumption for reasoning models surged 320 times while token costs fell only 80% year over year. In both cases, output quality was high while ROAI was effectively zero — a pattern this paper terms the ROAI trap. The paper formalises the ROAI ratio, derives a crossover theorem showing that ROAI-governed organisations outperform cost-per-token-governed organisations above an autonomy threshold ρ*, and demonstrates computationally that prompt engineering — reducing token cost without addressing fitness alignment — does not improve organisational fitness. These findings extend the IT business value literature (Melville, Kraemer, and Gurbaxani, 2004) and the AI productivity paradox literature (Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson, 2021) to the context of agentic AI deployment.

title: No Single Law, No Vacuum: Director Duties and AI Under Existing Canadian Law

detail.title: No Single Law, No Vacuum: Director Duties and AI Under Existing Canadian Law

declarations.ethicsApproval: This article reflects the law and regulatory developments as of June 2026, including the federal AI for All strategy (released June 4, 2026) and Bill C-36 (introduced June 15, 2026). Readers should note that Bill C-36 was at first reading at the time of writing and may be amended prior to enactment.

detail.abstract:
Canada does not have a single, comprehensive statute governing artificial intelligence. The proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act died on the order paper in January 2025 and has not been reintroduced. This absence is frequently treated, in both practice and commentary, as a regulatory gap. This article argues that it is not. 
The directors of Canadian corporations already owe duties that reach AI risk, grounded in the duty of care under section 122 of the Canada Business Corporations Act, and reinforced by provincial and federal privacy law, human rights and employment legislation, securities disclosure rules, and sector-specific prudential guidance such as the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' Guideline E-23. Drawing on Canada's newly released national AI strategy, the privacy reform introduced via Bill C-36, and two existing Canadian decisions (Moffatt v Air Canada and the Clearview AI litigation ), this article demonstrates that Canadian courts and regulators are already applying established legal principles to AI conduct, well ahead of any comprehensive AI statute. It closes with a practical governance framework for boards, in-house counsel, and compliance functions at financial institutions, mid-market companies, and private corporations, arguing that the absence of a single AI law is not a basis for delay but a more demanding standard of director conduct in its own right.

title: The Price of Exclusion: Regional Institutions and Sovereign Risk in a Currency Union
affiliations: University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business

detail.title: The Price of Exclusion: Regional Institutions and Sovereign Risk in a Currency Union
detail.abstract: What is the value of membership in an integrated financial architecture, and what does a sovereign lose when access to that architecture is withdrawn? We answer this question using the recent coup wave in the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU), which generated rare variation in sovereign access to a shared regional financial architecture while holding constant the common currency, central bank, sovereign debt market, banking system, and equity exchange. We show that markets price access rather than political turnover itself. Sovereigns experiencing access-preserving coups exhibit little durable repricing, whereas exclusion from the regional funding architecture generates a large and persistent sovereign re-entry premium. We interpret this premium as the revealed value of an institutional convenience yield associated with access to a shared investor base and market infrastructure. The effects extend beyond sovereign debt markets: bank equities embedded in the same financial architecture fall sharply at access loss but not at accesspreserving coups. We further provide suggestive evidence that exclusion is accompanied by creditor realignment rather than a collapse in foreign participation. Together, the results identify a previously difficult-to-measure financing benefit generated by membership in an integrated financial architecture and show how its loss is capitalized across sovereign debt and bank equity.

title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Bocconi University, Australian National University (ANU) and

detail.title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
detail.abstract: Behavioral interventions have become central to modern public policy, but their empirical promise remains contested because estimated treatment effects often appear small. We argue that a policy response is economically meaningful only relative to the response generated by alternative policies. We assemble more than 1,200 estimates from over 600 studies comparing "nudges" and traditional price interventions in the markets for cigarettes, alcohol, influenza vaccination, electricity, and residential water. Translating nudge effects into equivalent price changes, we find that behavioral interventions often correspond to enormous fiscal interventions, from an 11% tax on electricity to a 100% subsidy on influenza vaccinations. Nudges are also more cost-effective than price instruments in all markets, but cost-effectiveness does not predict the welfare ranking of policies. Using a behavioral extension of the Marginal Value of Public Funds, we show that nudges have high welfare returns at the margin, while price instruments often generate larger total surplus at scale.

title: Tax Incentives and Venture Capital Risk-Taking: Evidence from the QSBS Program
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and

detail.title: Tax Incentives and Venture Capital Risk-Taking: Evidence from the QSBS Program
detail.abstract: Do tax subsidies prompt investors to take on risk? We address this question by looking at investors' responses to changes to the Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) program, which reduces capital gains taxes on startup investing. We do so under a framework in which some startup investors — venture capitalists (VCs) — combine outside funding with incentive-based compensation, while others invest their own funds. Using bunching, triple-differences, and matching designs that exploit industry eligibility, investment vintage, and holding-period requirements, we analyze data from 158 thousand investor–firm pairings over two decades. We identify strategic investment timing, with subsidies prompting bunching at tax-eligible holding-period thresholds. Most notably, when and where tax subsidies apply, VCs shift their project selection toward riskier ventures: they invest more in pre-commercial stage startups, become more likely to provide startups with their initial capital, and invest more in startups with pre-existing debt, while becoming less likely to co-syndicate their investments. Tax-subsidized VC-backed ventures show higher failure rates, but on the flip side, attain higher valuations at exit and are more likely to reach "unicorn status." None of these patterns are observed for comparable non-VC investors in startups exposed to the same tax subsidies. Our tests further show that tax incentives lead to reallocation toward more innovative industries, yielding more impactful patents. Our study is the first to show that tax policy can shift entrepreneurial financing toward riskier, more innovative, and valuable startups.

title: Literature Review and Evidence Aggregation: A Toolkit for Applied Micro
affiliations: University of Chicago,  and University of Oxford

detail.title: Literature Review and Evidence Aggregation: A Toolkit for Applied Micro
detail.abstract: Consider an analyst interested in predicting the size of an effect. She has identified a set of prior published studies of similar effects. We provide a toolkit for (i) summarizing the prior literature, (ii) making predictions of effects in new contexts, and (iii) correcting for the bias from selectivity in the prior literature. We illustrate these methods with empirical examples from labor, public, behavioral, environmental, and development economics. Some of the tools are relevant even when only three prior studies are available. We show how it is possible to use covariates to transparently make predictions for a new context by reweighting prior estimates. The mean effect - after correcting for selectivity - is between 12% and 21% of the simple mean in our empirical examples. We conclude with a cookbook for practitioners producing meta-analyses.

title: Causal Inference for Social Network Formation
affiliations: University of Oxford, Harvard University and UCL School of Management, University College London

detail.title: Causal Inference for Social Network Formation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for identification, estimation, and inference on the causal mechanisms driving endogenous social network formation. Identification is challenging because of unobserved confounders and reverse causality; inference is complicated by questions of equilibrium and sampling. We leverage repeated observations of a network over time and random variation in initial ties to address challenges to causal identification. Our design-based approach sidesteps questions of sampling and asymptotics by treating both the set of nodes (individuals) and potential outcomes as non-random. We apply our approach to data from a large professional services firm, where new hires are randomly assigned to project teams within offices. We estimate the causal effect on tie formation of indirect ties, network degree, and local network density. Indirect ties have a strong and significant positive effect on tie formation, while the effects of degree and density are smaller and less robust.
